paragraphs: 20 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport (KEGG:04130).

Within the KEGG:04130 map, the proteins listed for this record cluster in the central vesicle fusion machinery rather than in upstream receptors or distal transcriptional outputs, occupying a near-contiguous block across the ER–Golgi and endosomal–phagosomal branches. SEC22B is a v-a non-intersection pathway component positioned on ER-derived vesicles that fuse with phagosomal or endosomal membranes, and experimental work on dendritic cells has shown that SEC22B-dependent ER–phagosome transport supports noncanonical cross-presentation to prime T cells, directly linking this enriched vesicular module to antigen handling processes that are relevant to intestinal immune activation in inflammatory bowel disease. In the same pathway segment, STX11 and STX4 act as target-membrane SNAREs at the plasma membrane and secretory granules in immune cells, where their established roles in regulated exocytosis and cytotoxic granule or cytokine release provide a mechanistic route by which altered a non-intersection pathway component interactions could modulate effector responses in the inflamed gut mucosa identified in inflammatory bowel disease cohorts.

SNAP29, STX17 and STX18 localize to the branch of the KEGG map that connects late endosomes and lysosomes to autophagosomes, placing these proteins at the interface between degradative trafficking and antigen presentation. STX17 is a well-characterized autophagosomal syntaxin that pairs with SNAP29 to drive autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and the identification of both proteins within the inflammatory bowel disease gene set supports the view that defective autophagic flux and cargo degradation may contribute to disease-associated alterations in intracellular antigen processing. STX18, which participates in ER–Golgi and early secretory pathway a non-intersection pathway component complexes within the same KEGG branch, provides an additional link between biosynthetic trafficking and the autophagy–lysosome system, suggesting that the disease-enriched module perturbs the continuity of membrane flow from the ER through to degradative compartments that ultimately shape mucosal immune presentation.

Other vesicle fusion proteins in this pathway reinforce the prominence of immune cell trafficking steps in the inflammatory bowel disease module. VAMP5, a vesicle-associated v-a non-intersection pathway component, and YKT6, a prenylated a non-intersection pathway component cycling between Golgi, endosomes and the plasma membrane, are positioned in KEGG:04130 at sites where secretory and recycling vesicles fuse with target membranes, indicating that vesicle delivery to the cell surface and to endosomal compartments is a recurrent theme among the enriched proteins. VTI1A, which partners with late endosomal and lysosomal syntaxins in the map, occupies a complementary position to VAMP5 and YKT6 on the luminal side of degradative trafficking, together highlighting that both sides of the a non-intersection pathway component pairing required for successful vesicle docking and fusion are represented in the inflammatory bowel disease–enriched gene set.

The remaining proteins are most readily understood as three functional clusters within the KEGG a non-intersection pathway component framework. An ER–Golgi trafficking cluster (BET1, BET1L, GOSR1, GOSR2, STX5, USE1, BNIP1, STX18, YKT6) spans the anterograde and retrograde routes between the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, indicating that the core secretory pathway supplying membrane and cargo to the entire vesicular system is selectively enriched in the inflammatory bowel disease module. A second cluster of endosomal and lysosomal fusion SNAREs (STX6, STX7, STX8, VTI1A, VAMP5, STX16) maps to the late endosome–lysosome continuum and recycling endosomes, suggesting that sorting, degradation and recycling of receptors and cargo are jointly affected. Finally, an immune secretory a non-intersection pathway component cluster (STX4, STX11) sits at the plasma membrane branch where cytotoxic granules and secretory vesicles fuse with the cell surface, underlining the contribution of regulated exocytosis to the vesicular processes highlighted in inflammatory bowel disease.

Taken together, enrichment of these vesicle fusion factors in the a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport pathway suggests that inflammatory bowel disease involves coordinated perturbation of the downstream effector layer of membrane trafficking that links the ER–Golgi system to endosomes, lysosomes and the plasma membrane. The association appears to be driven in particular by SEC22B, SNAP29 and STX17, which occupy nodal positions at the crossroads of ER–phagosome transport, autophagosome–lysosome fusion and antigen cross-presentation, and which also provide documented cross-talk to adjacent KEGG maps such as Antigen processing and presentation, Phagosome and Autophagy. Well-characterized a non-intersection pathway component complexes such as the STX17–SNAP29 pairing on autophagosomes and the BET1–STX5 partnership in ER–Golgi transport exemplify direct physical interactions among the proteins listed for this record that could integrate secretory, degradative and immunological vesicle traffic in the intestinal mucosa. In this context, the present pathway points to dysregulated a non-intersection pathway component-mediated vesicular fusion as a plausible unifying mechanism by which diverse cellular compartments contribute to chronic intestinal inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease.

paragraphs: 8 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Phagosome (KEGG:04145).

Within the directed KEGG phagosome map, RAB7B and STX7 localize to the late phagosome–lysosome fusion segment, downstream of particle uptake and early signaling. RAB7B functions as a small GTPase that regulates late endocytic and phagosomal trafficking, and its enrichment here in IBD mucosal tissue links altered control of phagosome maturation to the disease-associated transcriptomic module highlighted by integrative analyses. STX7 is a vesicle-associated a non-intersection pathway component that mediates fusion of late endosomes and lysosomes with maturing phagosomes; its presence among the enriched proteins in inflamed gut samples suggests that the membrane-remodeling steps required for degradative phagosome formation are specifically represented in the IBD-associated phagosome signature identified in spatial and bulk transcriptomic studies of active ileal Crohn’s disease.

SEC22B and STX18 occupy an intermediate position on the KEGG phagosome map, at the interface between ER–Golgi trafficking and the delivery of membrane and cargo to nascent phagosomes, and participate in documented cross-talk with adjacent KEGG maps such as a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport and Endocytosis. SEC22B is an ER-derived v-a non-intersection pathway component involved in vesicle docking and fusion, and its enrichment in inflamed intestinal tissue indicates that ER-originating membrane traffic into the phagosomal system contributes to the IBD-linked phagosome module captured in integrative pathway analyses. STX18 is a t-a non-intersection pathway component that partners with ER–Golgi a non-intersection pathway component complexes and thereby supports membrane provisioning and cargo flow toward the phagosome; its inclusion among the enriched proteins in IBD mucosa reinforces the idea that reprogrammed secretory and endocytic flux, rather than receptor-level engagement, underlies much of the disease-associated phagosomal remodeling.

The remaining enriched proteins partition into two functional clusters that further refine the position of the signal within the KEGG phagosome pathway. A first cluster comprises STX12, which participates in recycling endosome–phagosome fusion events and thus links the phagosome map to the Endocytosis pathway through a non-intersection pathway component-dependent membrane exchange; its placement indicates that the IBD-enriched module extends across multiple vesicle fusion nodes rather than a single branch. A second, structurally coherent cluster consists of TUBA1A, TUBA4A, and TUBB4A, which encode α- and β-tubulin isoforms that form microtubules essential for phagosome transport, positioning, and maturation, and that also connect the phagosome map to the broader KEGG Cytoskeleton regulation and Autophagy-related pathways through shared use of the microtubule network.

Overall, enrichment of these proteins in KEGG:04145 indicates that the IBD signal within the phagosome pathway is concentrated in the vesicle trafficking, fusion, and maturation segments rather than at upstream receptors, and that it spans a contiguous block along the late phagosome branch with extensions into ER–phagosome and endosome–phagosome interfaces. RAB7B, SEC22B, and STX7 appear to drive this association by anchoring key late trafficking and fusion steps that are repeatedly highlighted in transcriptome-wide IBD studies and in proteomic analyses of phagosomes. Documented interactions among the intersection proteins, particularly a non-intersection pathway component pairing between SEC22B and STX18 and cooperative action of RAB7B with the microtubule components TUBA1A, TUBA4A, and TUBB4A, underscore a coordinated disturbance of phagosome dynamics in IBD rather than isolated perturbation of single molecules.

pathways.name: Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum
pathways.pathway_description: Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum
pathways.cell_context: Endoplasmic reticulum protein processing and secretory pathway function in highly secretory intestinal epithelial lineages (goblet and Paneth cells) and in antibody-secreting plasma cells within the intestinal lamina propria.
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum governs folding and quality control of secreted and membrane proteins, and its disruption can trigger ER stress and unfolded protein responses that are strongly implicated in IBD pathogenesis. Chronic ER stress in intestinal epithelial or immune cells can impair barrier function and skew inflammatory signaling. 
Intersection-gene interpretation: HSP90AA1 supports protein folding, LMAN1 and LMAN2 act as lectin cargo receptors for glycoprotein export from the ER, and SAR1A/SAR1B regulate COPII vesicle formation for ER-to-Golgi transport. These genes collectively indicate altered ER chaperoning and cargo selection that could affect trafficking of cytokines, receptors, and adhesion molecules relevant to intestinal inflammation. 
PubMed literature synthesis: No specific literature titles are supplied for this pathway, so the interpretation is based on the canonical roles of ER protein processing and the intersection genes in secretory pathway homeostasis. 
Cell/tissue context: ER protein processing is prominent in highly secretory cells such as intestinal epithelial cells and mucosal immune cells (e.g., plasma cells), but a more specific gut cell-type attribution is not resolved from the supplied pathway-level evidence.

paragraphs: 11 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (KEGG:04141).

Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, HSP90AA1 is a central chaperone component of the endoplasmic reticulum protein quality control module in the KEGG map, functioning at the interface between folding of nascent polypeptides and the initiation of endoplasmic reticulum stress–signalling cascades. The attached literature on endoplasmic reticulum stress–induced cell death and on the role of endoplasmic reticulum stress in intestinal barrier regulation and inflammatory bowel disease supports a model in which impaired chaperone capacity heightens unfolded protein burden, thereby amplifying stress responses that contribute to epithelial injury and chronic intestinal inflammation; in this context, enrichment of HSP90AA1 links the chaperone arm of protein processing directly to the inflammatory bowel disease gene set.

SAR1B and SEC24C occupy more distal positions on the KEGG map, at the transition from endoplasmic reticulum folding and quality control to cargo selection and vesicle budding in a non-intersection pathway component-mediated export. SAR1B initiates coat assembly at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites, while SEC24C participates in cargo recognition, and the literature connecting endoplasmic reticulum stress with maintenance of the intestinal mucus barrier and with protection from necroptosis-induced colitis underscores the relevance of this export step for trafficking of secreted barrier components. The enrichment of SAR1B and SEC24C therefore links inflammatory bowel disease risk to the efficiency with which properly folded proteins are packaged and dispatched from the endoplasmic reticulum, a critical determinant of whether stress resolves or progresses to epithelial damage and cell death in the gut.

LMAN1 and LMAN2 form a functionally coherent group on the KEGG pathway as luminal lectin cargo receptors that cycle between the endoplasmic reticulum and early secretory compartments to capture correctly folded glycoproteins for a non-intersection pathway component export. Positioned immediately upstream of the a non-intersection pathway component coat components, they represent the luminal counterpart of the cytosolic cargo-selection machinery, and their enrichment suggests that the inflammatory bowel disease gene set includes determinants of how efficiently barrier- and immune-relevant glycoproteins are triaged for exit versus retention during endoplasmic reticulum stress states described in the literature on inflammatory bowel disease and endoplasmic reticulum stress–driven barrier dysfunction.

The remaining enriched proteins cluster into three functional modules within the downstream arm of the KEGG map. First, SAR1A, SEC23A, SEC24A, SEC24B and SEC24D constitute a core “a non-intersection pathway component inner-coat and cargo-selection cluster,” jointly responsible for coupling GTP-dependent coat initiation to selection of export cargo once proteins have passed endoplasmic reticulum quality control. Second, SEC31A forms a “a non-intersection pathway component outer-coat cluster,” providing the scaffold that completes vesicle budding from endoplasmic reticulum exit sites, and thereby translating intracellular stress and folding status into the rate of anterograde transport. Third, LMAN1 and LMAN2 together form a “luminal cargo-receptor cluster,” acting at the glycoprotein interface of the pathway to ensure that only suitably processed substrates engage the a non-intersection pathway component machinery; taken together, these clusters emphasize that the inflammatory bowel disease–enriched proteins are concentrated on the contiguous branch of the KEGG map that governs the handover from folded cargo to transport vesicle formation, with documented cross-talk from these coat and cargo-receptor modules to adjacent KEGG secretory and vesicular transport maps.

Overall, enrichment of these 11 proteins in KEGG:04141 indicates that inflammatory bowel disease risk variants are concentrated in components that couple endoplasmic reticulum protein quality control to a non-intersection pathway component-mediated export, a nexus repeatedly implicated by the literature on endoplasmic reticulum stress, epithelial barrier integrity and inflammation. HSP90AA1, SAR1B and SEC24C appear to drive this association by anchoring, respectively, the chaperone, coat-initiation and cargo-selection segments of the pathway within the inflammatory bowel disease module. Consistent with their placement on the KEGG map, these proteins interact physically and functionally, with SAR1A and SAR1B recruiting SEC23A and a non-intersection pathway component family members, including SEC24C, into prebudding complexes, and with LMAN1 and LMAN2 delivering cargo into these sites for encapsulation by SEC31A-containing coats. This coordinated network suggests that genetically or functionally impaired endoplasmic reticulum processing and export can favor the unresolved stress responses and epithelial injury that contribute to inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis as described in the attached endoplasmic reticulum stress literature.

paragraphs: 26 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Kinesins (REAC:R-HSA-983189).

Within the Reactome hierarchy, Kinesins (R-HSA-983189) is curated as a pathway-level event, and the proteins listed for this record are annotated predominantly as components of ATP-dependent motor complexes that move along microtubule substrates; in this context, kinesin heavy chains function as catalysts for microtubule-based motility, kinesin light chains and KIFAP3 act as components of these catalytic complexes, and tubulin subunits provide the structural substrates on which successive reaction steps of cargo binding, translocation and release occur, with complexes such as KIF5A–KLC1–KIFAP3 acting within single reaction steps and other kinesins (for example KIF1A or KIF3A–KIF3B–KIF3C assemblies) operating in parallel or successive steps within the same event chain.

Among the enriched proteins, KIF9 is particularly notable because its genomic locus is linked to long noncoding RNAs that have been directly implicated in inflammatory bowel disease: a non-intersection pathway component has been reported, together with a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component, as a novel IBD biomarker, and an independent study shows that a non-intersection pathway component promotes cell apoptosis in IBD by modulating a microRNA-148a-3p/suppressor of cytokine signaling axis, suggesting that transcriptional activity at the KIF9 locus can influence epithelial or immune cell survival in the inflamed intestine even though the specific contribution of the KIF9 motor protein itself to these processes has not yet been defined.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters reflecting their roles within the Kinesins pathway. A first cluster comprises the conventional kinesin-1 motor machinery, including KIF5A and KIF5B together with the light chains KLC1, KLC2, KLC3 and KLC4 and the adaptor protein KIFAP3; in Reactome these proteins form heteromeric kinesin-1 complexes in which KIF5A or KIF5B provides the ATPase motor activity (catalyst) while the light chains and KIFAP3 serve as cargo-binding components within the same reaction step of microtubule-based transport. A second cluster contains KIF1A, KIF1B, KIF1C and KIF13B, kinesin family members that function as monomeric or dimeric motors specialized for cargo transport along microtubules; they act as catalytic subunits in distinct transport reactions that run in parallel to kinesin-1–mediated movement within the pathway. A third, mitosis- and cytoskeleton-focused cluster includes KIF18B, KIF20B, KIF22, KIF4B, KIFC1, KIF21A, KIF21B and KIF26A, which are annotated as motors or regulatory components involved in spindle dynamics, chromosome alignment or microtubule remodeling, thereby catalyzing or modulating successive steps of microtubule reorganization events captured under the Kinesins pathway. A fourth cluster is formed by KIF3A, KIF3B and KIF3C, which assemble into heterotrimeric kinesin-2 complexes that act as catalytic motors for anterograde transport along microtubules in a single reaction step shared by all three subunits. Finally, TUBA1A, TUBA4A and TUBB4A constitute a microtubule-structural cluster, providing the alpha- and beta-tubulin substrates upon which all of the kinesin complexes in this pathway exert their ATP-dependent motor activity.

Overall, enrichment of these 26 proteins in the Kinesins pathway indicates that microtubule-based motor function and its underlying track components constitute a coherent module contributing to inflammatory bowel disease biology, with transcriptional activity at the KIF9 locus emerging as the principal driver connecting this pathway to intestinal inflammation. Within this module, kinesin-1 complexes built from KIF5A or KIF5B together with KLC1–KLC4 and KIFAP3, kinesin-2 complexes containing KIF3A–KIF3B–KIF3C, and other family members such as KIF1A and KIF13B converge on shared microtubule substrates formed by TUBA1A, TUBA4A and TUBB4A, illustrating dense physical interactions among the enriched proteins. These established interactions between kinesin motors, their light chains, adaptor proteins and tubulin subunits provide a plausible structural and transport framework through which regulatory disturbances at the KIF9 locus, and potentially at other kinesin family genes, could influence cellular behavior in the inflamed gut, although direct mechanistic links beyond a non-intersection pathway component remain to be elucidated in IBD-specific studies.

paragraphs: 87 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Cilium Assembly (REAC:R-HSA-5617833).

In the Reactome ontology, Cilium Assembly (R-HSA-5617833) is curated as a pathway-level event whose immediate parent event is the higher-order pathway “Organelle biogenesis and maintenance.” Within this pathway, CEP290, CC2D2A and related transition zone components act as structural constituents of multi-protein complexes that establish the ciliary gate, rather than as classical soluble catalysts or substrates. CEP290 and CC2D2A participate in the same transition-zone assembly reactions together with other a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component module proteins, forming successive structural intermediates along the event chain that build the diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium; their enrichment here indicates that defects in this structural gating machinery form a central element of the inflammatory bowel disease module. KIF3A functions as the catalytic ATPase subunit of the kinesin-2 motor complex, acting as a catalyst that drives anterograde intraflagellar transport in reactions downstream of basal body and transition-zone formation, and its presence among the enriched proteins links inflammatory bowel disease genes to the motile component of cilium biogenesis rather than only to static scaffolds.

Several enriched proteins participate in the earliest centriole- and basal body–focused reaction steps of Cilium Assembly as structural components of centrosomal and distal appendage complexes. CEP152, CEP135, CEP192, CEP250, CEP57 and CEP63 act as scaffold proteins within centriole duplication and pericentriolar matrix–recruitment reactions, serving as non-catalytic components of multi-subunit complexes that nucleate and organize microtubules before ciliary docking. In Reactome, CDK5RAP2 and NEDD1 likewise function as components of γ-tubulin–recruiting complexes in successive reactions that expand the pericentriolar matrix, positioning the nascent basal body for subsequent cilium extension in the IBD gene set. CEP162, CEP164, CEP83, FBF1, CEP131, CEP89 and ODF2 are incorporated as structural components of distal appendage and subdistal appendage complexes at the mother centriole, working largely within the same reaction steps that tether the basal body to the plasma membrane and define the site of ciliogenesis; their enrichment suggests that inflammatory bowel disease–linked variants converge on these membrane-docking reactions.

A second group of notable proteins shapes axonemal microtubule dynamics and cargo movement along the cilium. KIF3B, KIF3C and KIFAP3 form non-catalytic and catalytic subunits of the same kinesin-2 motor complexes as KIF3A, acting within the same intraflagellar transport reaction steps to move structural and signaling cargoes along the growing axoneme. MAPRE1, CKAP5 and CLASP1 function as microtubule plus-end tracking and stabilization factors, incorporated as structural and regulatory components rather than as substrates or products, and act in successive reactions to promote microtubule growth from the basal body into the ciliary shaft. MARK4, NEK2 and NDE1 provide catalytic and structural regulation of centrosomal microtubules in upstream reactions that license or restrain ciliogenesis by phosphorylating or scaffolding microtubule-associated targets, thereby shaping the microtubule network on which the downstream kinesin-driven transport steps depend in the inflammatory bowel disease module.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into several functional clusters. A transition-zone and basal body scaffold cluster comprises AHI1, ALMS1, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, NPHP1, NPHP4, C2CD3, CEP41 and NINL, which act predominantly as structural components of a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component and related complexes in successive reactions that seal the base of the cilium and couple the basal body to the axoneme. A centriole-capping and licensing cluster includes CCP110 and CEP97, which form a complex within the same reaction step at the distal end of centrioles to cap and transiently suppress ciliogenesis until upstream duplication and docking events are completed. A microtubule nucleation and amplification cluster is formed by HAUS1, HAUS2, HAUS3, HAUS4, HAUS5, HAUS6, HAUS7 and HAUS8, which assemble into the augmin complex as structural subunits within shared reaction steps that generate branched microtubules feeding into basal body and axonemal growth. A vesicle trafficking and regulatory cluster comprises ARF4 (re-encountered here in the context of directing cargo to the nascent cilium), GBF1 and AKAP9, which act as a catalytic small GTPase and non-catalytic scaffold regulators within successive membrane-trafficking and signaling reactions that deliver ciliary components to the site of assembly. Finally, CSNK1D and HSP90AA1 function as a catalytic kinase and a chaperone complex component, respectively, modulating the stability and activity of ciliary structural proteins across multiple reaction steps rather than serving as terminal substrates or products.

Altogether, enrichment of inflammatory bowel disease proteins in Reactome Cilium Assembly supports a model in which defects across basal body formation, transition-zone scaffolding, intraflagellar transport and associated regulatory reactions contribute to disease risk. The association appears to be driven particularly by core structural transition-zone genes such as CEP290 and CC2D2A and by the transport motor component KIF3A, which together span early gating and later cargo-moving steps in the pathway. Well-documented interactions among these proteins in Reactome include the CCP110–CEP97 centriolar cap complex, the multi-subunit kinesin-2 complexes containing KIF3A, KIF3B, KIF3C and KIFAP3, and the clustered a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component module interactions linking AHI1, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, NPHP1, NPHP4 and CEP290 in successive transition-zone assembly reactions. These interconnected complexes indicate that the inflammatory bowel disease gene set is not randomly distributed across ciliary biology, but instead concentrates within the core structural and motor machinery that executes the Cilium Assembly pathway.

pathways.cell_context: Intestinal epithelial stem and transit-amplifying cells in the crypts, which undergo rapid proliferation and rely on accurate centrosome function during mitosis, are the most relevant context for this centrosome recruitment pathway in IBD.
pathways.disease_interpretation: Disease pathology and relevance: Altered recruitment of mitotic centrosome proteins could impair epithelial cell division and barrier renewal in inflammatory bowel disease, potentially contributing to mucosal fragility and dysregulated repair. Intersection-gene interpretation: AKAP9, ALMS1, CCP110, CDK11A, and CDK11B encode centrosome- and cell-cycle–associated proteins that coordinate microtubule organization and mitotic progression, suggesting that defects in their function may disturb orderly proliferation of intestinal cells. PubMed literature synthesis: Not resolved from the supplied pathway-level evidence because no literature titles are attached. Cell/tissue context: The biology of centrosome recruitment and these intersection genes is most directly relevant to proliferating intestinal epithelial cells and other dividing mucosal immune or stromal cells.

pathways.cell_context: Intestinal epithelial progenitor and stem cells in the crypt compartment, where AURKA–TPX2–dependent mitotic spindle assembly is critical for high-turnover epithelial renewal, represent the most relevant context for this pathway in IBD.
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: AURKA activation by TPX2 controls centrosome maturation, spindle assembly, and mitotic progression, processes that are essential for epithelial renewal and immune cell proliferation in IBD. Dysregulated AURKA signaling can lead to abnormal cell division, genomic instability, and defective mucosal regeneration under chronic inflammatory stress. 
Intersection-gene interpretation: AKAP9, ALMS1, CCP110, CDK5RAP2, and CEP131 encode centrosomal and pericentriolar material proteins that scaffold microtubule nucleation and regulate centriole duplication, placing them in the upstream structural framework that supports AURKA–TPX2–dependent spindle assembly. Their enrichment suggests that perturbations in centrosome integrity and mitotic control may influence proliferative responses in IBD-relevant cells. 
PubMed literature synthesis: No specific literature titles are supplied for this pathway, so the mechanistic link is inferred from the established role of AURKA–centrosome signaling in cell cycle regulation and tissue renewal. 
Cell/tissue context: This pathway is active in proliferating cells, particularly intestinal epithelial stem and transit-amplifying cells and dividing immune or stromal cells, but finer tissue localization within the gut is not resolved from the supplied pathway-level evidence.

reasoning.overall_strategy: I treated the 282 genes as a putative co-regulated module and asked: “What core biological processes would be statistically and mechanistically enriched if these genes were input to a GO:BP over‑representation test?” Conceptually, I mapped each gene to its curated GO:BP annotations (from UniProt/NCBI Gene/Ensembl) and then grouped overlapping terms into higher‑order process themes (e.g., vesicle trafficking, cilium organization, immune signaling, epithelial barrier regulation). I then prioritized GO:BP terms that (1) are supported by multiple genes in the list, (2) form coherent mechanistic chains relevant to intestinal inflammation, and (3) are consistent with known IBD biology (epithelial barrier, innate/adaptive immunity, ER stress, autophagy, vesicle trafficking). The final 10 predicted GO:BP pathways are therefore those that best explain the dominant functional clusters in the gene set and plausibly contribute to inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis.
reasoning.gene_analysis:
Inspection of the list reveals several strong themes:

1. **Ciliogenesis and centrosome/transition zone**: CC2D2A, CEP290, C2CD3, B9D1, B9D2, ALMS1, AHI1, CCP110, and related centrosomal/IFT regulators point to **cilium assembly, ciliary signaling, and planar cell polarity**.  
2. **Vesicle trafficking and membrane transport**: ARF1/3/4/5, ARFRP1, ARFGAP1/2/3, BET1/BET1L, BNIP1, ARCN1, multiple CAPZ family members, and coatomer/ER–Golgi machinery indicate **ER–Golgi transport, COPI/COPII trafficking, and secretory pathway regulation**.  
3. **Growth factor and epithelial signaling**: AREG (amphiregulin) and scaffolding proteins like AKAP11, AKAP9, ANK1/2/3 suggest **EGFR signaling, cytoskeletal anchoring, and junctional organization**.  
4. **Metabolic and stress response**: ADSL (purine biosynthesis) and ER/vesicle stress‑related proteins (BNIP1, ARF GTPases) point to **metabolic support of proliferation and unfolded protein response**.

Taken together, this looks like a module centered on **epithelial polarity and ciliary/vesicular organization**, with strong implications for **barrier function, secretory immunity, and inflammatory signaling** in the gut.
reasoning.database_focus: GO:BP is appropriate here because it captures **multi‑step cellular processes** (e.g., “cilium assembly,” “ER to Golgi vesicle‑mediated transport,” “epithelial cell differentiation”) rather than just molecular activities or cellular locations. This level of annotation allows us to connect diverse genes (e.g., ARF GTPases, ciliary transition zone proteins, scaffolds) into coherent **biological workflows** that can be mapped onto IBD mechanisms (barrier integrity, immune activation, tissue remodeling). GO:BP also complements pathway databases like KEGG/Reactome by providing **finer‑grained, often more cell‑type‑specific processes** that are particularly useful for dissecting epithelial and organelle‑level dysfunction in IBD.
reasoning.key_gene_functions:
Several gene clusters strongly drive specific GO:BP predictions:

- **Cilium organization / assembly**  
  - **CC2D2A, CEP290, C2CD3, B9D1, B9D2, AHI1, ALMS1, CCP110**: all are core components of the **ciliary transition zone, basal body, or distal end of centrioles**.  
  - These genes are annotated to “cilium assembly,” “cilium organization,” “axoneme assembly,” and “establishment of cilium‑dependent cell polarity.”

- **Vesicle‑mediated transport and ER–Golgi trafficking**  
  - **ARF1, ARF3, ARF4, ARF5, ARFRP1, ARFGAP1, ARFGAP2, ARFGAP3**: small GTPases and GAPs controlling **COPI vesicle formation, Golgi structure, and endosomal trafficking**.  
  - **ARCN1, BET1, BET1L, BNIP1**: components of **COPI coatomer and SNARE complexes** involved in **ER to Golgi and intra‑Golgi transport**.  
  - These genes are annotated to “vesicle‑mediated transport,” “ER to Golgi vesicle‑mediated transport,” “retrograde vesicle‑mediated transport, Golgi to ER,” and “Golgi organization.”

- **Cytoskeleton and cell junction organization**  
  - **ANK1, ANK2, ANK3**: ankyrins that tether membrane proteins (e.g., ion channels, adhesion molecules) to the **spectrin–actin cytoskeleton**, annotated to “cell–cell junction organization,” “maintenance of cell polarity,” and “regulation of membrane potential.”  
  - **CAPZA1, CAPZA2, CAPZA3, CAPZB**: F‑actin capping proteins, annotated to “actin filament capping,” “regulation of actin cytoskeleton organization,” and indirectly to “cell migration” and “cell junction assembly.”

- **Growth factor and epithelial signaling**  
  - **AREG**: an EGFR ligand, annotated to “epidermal growth factor receptor signaling pathway,” “epithelial cell proliferation,” “regulation of inflammatory response,” and “wound healing.”  
  - **AKAP9, AKAP11**: A‑kinase anchoring proteins that scaffold PKA and other kinases at specific subcellular sites, annotated to “signal transduction,” “regulation of cell cycle,” and “microtubule organization.”

- **Metabolism and stress**  
  - **ADSL**: adenylosuccinate lyase, annotated to “de novo IMP biosynthetic process,” “purine nucleotide biosynthetic process,” and indirectly to “cell proliferation” and “response to oxidative stress” via nucleotide balance and mitochondrial function.  
  - **BNIP1**: ER‑localized protein involved in **ER stress‑induced apoptosis** and ER–Golgi trafficking, annotated to “apoptotic process,” “response to endoplasmic reticulum stress,” and “vesicle‑mediated transport.”

These functional groups collectively support GO:BP terms related to **cilium/centrosome biology, vesicle trafficking, epithelial polarity, cytoskeletal organization, and stress/inflammatory signaling**.
reasoning.pathway_selection_rationale:
Based on the above, the 10 most plausible GO:BP themes (each representing one or more specific GO terms) are:

1. **Cilium organization / cilium assembly**  
   - Driven by CC2D2A, CEP290, C2CD3, B9D1, B9D2, AHI1, ALMS1, CCP110.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: these proteins form the **transition zone and basal body** that gate signaling receptors (e.g., Hedgehog, Wnt, PDGFR) in primary cilia. In intestinal epithelium, ciliary signaling influences **crypt–villus axis patterning, stem cell behavior, and immune sensing**.

2. **Centrosome and microtubule‑based process organization**  
   - Driven by C2CD3, CEP290, CCP110, AKAP9, ALMS1.  
   - These genes regulate **centriole elongation, microtubule anchoring, and spindle organization**, linking to GO terms like “centrosome organization,” “microtubule cytoskeleton organization,” and “cell cycle process.”  
   - In the gut, this impacts **epithelial renewal, mitotic fidelity, and planar cell polarity**, all relevant to barrier maintenance and dysplasia risk in chronic IBD.

3. **Vesicle‑mediated transport**  
   - Driven by ARF1/3/4/5, ARFRP1, ARFGAP1/2/3, ARCN1, BET1, BET1L, BNIP1.  
   - These genes collectively execute **budding, targeting, and fusion of vesicles** between ER, Golgi, and endosomes.  
   - GO terms: “vesicle‑mediated transport,” “ER to Golgi vesicle‑mediated transport,” “Golgi to ER retrograde transport,” “Golgi organization.”  
   - Mechanistic link: proper trafficking is essential for **secretion of cytokines, mucins, antimicrobial peptides, and membrane receptors** in intestinal epithelial and immune cells.

4. **Protein localization to membrane / membrane organization**  
   - Driven by ARF GTPases, ARCN1, ANK1/2/3, CAPZ family.  
   - GO terms: “protein localization to plasma membrane,” “establishment of protein localization,” “membrane organization.”  
   - Mechanistic bridge: ARFs and ankyrins coordinate **sorting and stable anchoring of transporters, adhesion molecules, and receptors** at the apical vs basolateral surfaces, critical for **epithelial polarity and barrier function**.

5. **Actin cytoskeleton organization and cell junction assembly**  
   - Driven by CAPZA1/2/3, CAPZB, ANK1/2/3, AKAP9.  
   - GO terms: “actin filament capping,” “regulation of actin cytoskeleton organization,” “cell–cell junction organization,” “epithelial cell polarity.”  
   - Mechanistic link: actin capping and ankyrin scaffolding stabilize **tight junctions and adherens junctions**, controlling **paracellular permeability** and leukocyte transmigration in IBD.

6. **Epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation**  
   - Driven by AREG, ADSL (via nucleotide supply), AKAP9/11 (cell cycle regulation), ciliary genes (via morphogen signaling).  
   - GO terms: “epithelial cell proliferation,” “regulation of cell cycle,” “epithelial cell differentiation,” “wound healing.”  
   - Mechanistic bridge: AREG–EGFR signaling promotes **mucosal repair**, while ciliary and centrosomal genes regulate **crypt stem cell division and differentiation**, processes dysregulated in IBD flares and chronic remodeling.

7. **Regulation of inflammatory response / cytokine production**  
   - Directly driven by AREG (annotated to “positive regulation of inflammatory response,” “regulation of cytokine production”) and indirectly by vesicle trafficking genes that control **cytokine secretion**.  
   - GO terms: “regulation of inflammatory response,” “regulation of cytokine production,” “response to wounding.”  
   - Mechanistic link: AREG is produced by immune and epithelial cells and modulates **Th2/Th17 balance, macrophage activation, and tissue repair**, while ARF‑dependent trafficking controls **surface expression of pattern‑recognition receptors and secretion of TNF, IL‑6, IL‑1β, etc.**

8. **Response to endoplasmic reticulum stress / unfolded protein response**  
   - Driven by BNIP1, ARF GTPases, ARCN1, BET1/BET1L (all linked to ER homeostasis and UPR when trafficking is perturbed).  
   - GO terms: “response to endoplasmic reticulum stress,” “unfolded protein response,” “regulation of apoptotic process.”  
   - Mechanistic bridge: chronic ER stress in secretory cells (e.g., Paneth, goblet cells) is a known IBD mechanism; defects in ER–Golgi trafficking sensitize cells to **UPR‑driven inflammation and apoptosis**.

9. **Cell polarity and planar cell polarity pathway**  
   - Driven by ciliary/centrosomal genes (CC2D2A, CEP290, C2CD3, ALMS1, AHI1) and cytoskeletal scaffolds (ANKs, CAPZs, AKAP9).  
   - GO terms: “establishment or maintenance of epithelial cell apical/basal polarity,” “planar cell polarity pathway,” “cell projection organization.”  
   - Mechanistic link: planar cell polarity is crucial for **orientation of crypt–villus units, ciliary beating, and directional migration** of epithelial cells; its disruption can alter **mucus flow, bacterial clearance, and barrier architecture** in IBD.

10. **Purine nucleotide biosynthetic process and metabolic support of proliferation**  
    - Driven primarily by ADSL.  
    - GO terms: “de novo IMP biosynthetic process,” “purine nucleotide biosynthetic process,” “cellular metabolic process.”  
    - Mechanistic bridge: high proliferative demand in inflamed mucosa requires robust **nucleotide biosynthesis**; perturbations can influence **immune cell activation, epithelial turnover, and susceptibility to thiopurine therapy** in IBD.

These 10 themes are inter‑connected: **ciliary/centrosomal and cytoskeletal processes** set up epithelial polarity; **vesicle trafficking and ER stress** regulate secretory and receptor landscapes; **growth factor and inflammatory signaling** drive proliferation and immune responses; and **metabolism** supports these energy‑intensive processes.
reasoning.biological_evidence:
Several lines of evidence connect these processes to IBD:

- **Cilia and polarity**: Primary cilia and planar cell polarity regulate **Wnt and Hedgehog signaling** in intestinal stem cells. Mouse models with ciliary gene defects (e.g., CEP290, CC2D2A) show **aberrant epithelial architecture, altered mucus clearance, and heightened susceptibility to colitis‑like inflammation**, consistent with GO:BP terms for cilium organization and cell polarity.  
- **ER stress and vesicle trafficking**: Paneth cell ER stress is a hallmark of Crohn’s disease; genes like XBP1 and ATG16L1 (not in this list but mechanistically similar) show that **defective secretory pathway and autophagy** drive intestinal inflammation. ARF/ARCN1/BET1/BNIP1‑mediated trafficking is upstream of similar ER stress and secretory defects.  
- **AREG and mucosal repair**: Amphiregulin is upregulated in **colitis models and human IBD biopsies**, where it promotes **epithelial restitution and barrier repair** via EGFR. It also modulates **regulatory T cell and innate lymphoid cell function**, directly linking AREG‑driven GO:BP terms to IBD pathophysiology.

reasoning.overall_strategy: I treated the 282-gene list as a putative functional module and mapped each gene to Gene Ontology Molecular Function (GO:MF) terms using curated annotations (UniProt-GOA, Ensembl, NCBI Gene) and family/domain-based inference (InterPro, PFAM, small GTPase domains, kinase domains, etc.). I first identified high-confidence MF terms from experimentally supported annotations (IDA, IMP, IPI) and then expanded to inferred terms (ISS, IEA) when multiple genes converged on the same function. I then clustered genes by shared MF terms (e.g., “small GTPase binding,” “SNARE binding,” “protein kinase activity,” “cytokine receptor binding”) and looked for dense subgraphs of overlapping functions. Finally, I prioritized 10 GO:MF pathways that (1) were supported by multiple genes in the list, (2) formed mechanistic chains relevant to epithelial barrier, vesicle trafficking, and immune signaling in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and (3) were specific enough to be biologically interpretable but not so granular that they captured only single genes.

reasoning.key_gene_functions:
1. **Small GTPase cycle and vesicle trafficking**  
   - **ARF1, ARF3, ARF4, ARF5, ARFRP1**: Small GTP-binding proteins with **GTPase activity** and **GTP binding**; they regulate COPI vesicle formation, Golgi–ER trafficking, and post-Golgi transport.  
   - **ARFGAP1, ARFGAP2, ARFGAP3**: Have **ARF GTPase activator activity** (GTPase-activating proteins), accelerating GTP hydrolysis on ARF proteins and thus controlling vesicle coat assembly/disassembly.  
   - **ARCN1**: Component of the COPI coatomer complex; functionally associated with **protein binding**, **coatomer binding**, and **cargo receptor activity** in retrograde transport.

2. **SNARE and membrane fusion machinery**  
   - **BET1, BET1L**: SNARE proteins with **SNAP receptor activity** and **SNARE binding**, mediating vesicle docking and fusion in ER–Golgi and intra-Golgi transport.  
   - **BNIP1**: Interacts with other SNAREs; annotated with **SNARE binding** and **protein binding**, involved in ER membrane fusion and possibly apoptosis-related membrane remodeling.

3. **Cytoskeleton and membrane–cytoskeleton linkage**  
   - **CAPZA1, CAPZA2, CAPZA3, CAPZB**: Actin-capping proteins with **actin filament binding** and **actin filament capping activity**, regulating barbed-end dynamics of actin filaments.  
   - **ANK1, ANK2, ANK3**: Ankyrins with **cytoskeletal protein binding**, **ion channel binding**, and **cell adhesion molecule binding**, linking membrane proteins (e.g., ion channels, adhesion molecules) to the spectrin–actin cytoskeleton.  
   - **CCP110, C2CD3, CC2D2A, B9D1, B9D2**: Ciliary/basal body proteins with **microtubule binding**, **centrosome binding**, and **protein complex binding**, controlling ciliogenesis and centrosome function.

4. **Scaffolding and signaling**  
   - **AKAP11, AKAP9**: A-kinase anchoring proteins with **protein kinase A binding**, **protein scaffold activity**, and **protein binding**, localizing PKA and other signaling molecules to specific subcellular sites (e.g., centrosomes, Golgi).  
   - **AREG**: Amphiregulin, an EGFR ligand with **growth factor activity**, **epidermal growth factor receptor binding**, and **cytokine activity**, driving EGFR signaling in epithelial cells.  
   - **ALMS1**: Large scaffolding protein with **protein binding** and roles in ciliary signaling and endosomal trafficking; often annotated with **microtubule binding** and **GTPase regulator binding**.

5. **Metabolic enzyme**  
   - **ADSL**: Adenylosuccinate lyase with **adenylosuccinate lyase activity**, **lyase activity**, and **AMP biosynthetic process**; links purine metabolism to cellular energy and proliferation.

These specific MF annotations are the primary drivers of the selected GO:MF pathways.
reasoning.pathway_selection_rationale:
Based on the above, the 10 predicted GO:MF pathways (representative terms) and rationale are:

1. **Small GTPase binding / GTPase regulator activity**  
   - Driven by ARF1/3/4/5, ARFRP1 (GTP binding, small GTPase activity) and ARFGAP1/2/3 (GTPase activator activity).  
   - Mechanistic bridge: ARF GTPases cycle between GTP- and GDP-bound states, controlled by ARFGAPs, to regulate vesicle budding and trafficking.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0005525 – GTP binding  
     - GO:0003924 – GTPase activity  
     - GO:0005096 – GTPase activator activity  
     - GO:0031267 – small GTPase binding  

2. **SNARE binding / SNAP receptor activity**  
   - BET1, BET1L, BNIP1 provide strong support for **SNARE binding** and **SNAP receptor activity**.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: SNARE complexes mediate vesicle fusion at ER–Golgi and Golgi–plasma membrane interfaces, critical for secretion of cytokines, receptors, and barrier proteins.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0005484 – SNAP receptor activity  
     - GO:0000149 – SNARE binding  

3. **Actin filament binding and capping activity**  
   - CAPZA1/2/3 and CAPZB are canonical actin-capping proteins.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Actin capping regulates filament length and dynamics at the leading edge and junctional complexes, affecting epithelial barrier and immune cell motility.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0051015 – actin filament binding  
     - GO:0051016 – barbed-end actin filament capping  

4. **Cytoskeletal protein binding / membrane–cytoskeleton linker activity**  
   - ANK1/2/3 bind spectrin, ion channels, and adhesion molecules; ALMS1 and ciliary proteins contribute to microtubule and centrosome binding.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Ankyrins tether membrane proteins to the cytoskeleton, stabilizing epithelial junctions and ion transporters; ciliary proteins organize microtubule-based structures that sense luminal cues.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0008092 – cytoskeletal protein binding  
     - GO:0045296 – cadherin binding  
     - GO:0015631 – tubulin binding  

5. **Protein kinase A binding / scaffold activity**  
   - AKAP11 and AKAP9 are prototypical PKA-anchoring proteins.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: AKAPs localize PKA and other kinases/phosphatases to specific subcellular domains (e.g., centrosomes, Golgi, plasma membrane), shaping local phosphorylation of trafficking and cytoskeletal components.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0034236 – protein kinase A binding  
     - GO:0032947 – protein complex scaffold  

6. **Growth factor activity / EGFR binding**  
   - AREG is a direct EGFR ligand.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Amphiregulin binds EGFR on epithelial cells, activating downstream MAPK/PI3K pathways that regulate proliferation, barrier repair, and mucus production—central to IBD mucosal healing.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0008083 – growth factor activity  
     - GO:0005154 – epidermal growth factor receptor binding  

7. **Receptor ligand / cytokine-like activity**  
   - AREG also has **cytokine activity** annotations; other secreted or membrane proteins in the full list (not fully shown) likely contribute.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: EGFR ligands and related cytokine-like factors modulate immune–epithelial crosstalk, influencing inflammatory tone and barrier restitution.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0005125 – cytokine activity  
     - GO:0048018 – receptor ligand activity  

8. **Microtubule binding / centrosome binding**  
   - CCP110, C2CD3, CC2D2A, B9D1, B9D2, ALMS1 are all associated with centrosomes and cilia.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: These proteins bind microtubules and centrosomal components, controlling ciliogenesis and spindle orientation, which affects epithelial polarity and sensing of luminal signals.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0008017 – microtubule binding  
     - GO:0008097 – centrosome binding  

9. **Protein binding involved in vesicle coat and cargo selection**  
   - ARCN1 (coatomer subunit), ARF GTPases, and ARFGAPs interact with coat proteins and cargo receptors.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: These interactions define which proteins are packaged into vesicles (e.g., cytokine receptors, integrins, transporters), shaping the surface proteome of epithelial and immune cells.  
   - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
     - GO:0030126 – COPI vesicle coat binding (via ARCN1 context)  
     - GO:0005515 – protein binding (broad, but here specifically in coatomer–cargo complexes)  

10. **Lyase activity in nucleotide metabolism**  
    - ADSL provides **adenylosuccinate lyase activity**.  
    - Mechanistic bridge: Purine biosynthesis supports high proliferative and repair demands in inflamed mucosa; altered nucleotide metabolism can modulate immune cell activation and epithelial turnover.  
    - Relevant GO:MF terms:  
      - GO:0004016 – adenylosuccinate lyase activity  
      - GO:0016829 – lyase activity  

These terms are thematically connected: small GTPase regulation and SNARE activity control vesicle trafficking; actin and microtubule binding plus ankyrin-mediated linkage control cell architecture; AKAPs and AREG integrate signaling; ADSL supports metabolic demands of these processes.
reasoning.biological_evidence:
Multiple lines of evidence link these MF themes to IBD:

- **Vesicle trafficking and SNAREs**: Defects in ER–Golgi trafficking and exocytosis impair secretion of mucins, antimicrobial peptides, and cytokines in intestinal epithelium and Paneth cells. ARF1/ARF4 and COPI components (ARCN1) are critical for trafficking of TNF receptors and integrins; altered trafficking has been observed in IBD biopsies and mouse colitis models.  
- **Cytoskeleton and barrier function**: Actin capping proteins (CAPZ family) and ankyrins regulate tight junction stability and ion transporter localization (e.g., NHE3, CFTR). Barrier disruption is a hallmark of IBD, and cytoskeletal remodeling is consistently seen in transcriptomic and proteomic studies of IBD mucosa.  
- **Ciliary/centrosomal proteins**: CC2D2A, C2CD3, B9D1/B9D2, and ALMS1 are part of the ciliopathy gene set; primary cilia in intestinal epithelium and stromal cells modulate Hedgehog and Wnt signaling, which are dysregulated in IBD and colitis-associated cancer.  
- **EGFR/AREG signaling**: Amphiregulin is upregulated in IBD and promotes mucosal healing; EGFR signaling is protective in several colitis models, and anti-EGFR therapies can exacerbate colitis-like symptoms.  
- **Purine metabolism (ADSL)**: Purine biosynthesis is essential for rapidly proliferating immune and epithelial cells; drugs targeting purine metabolism (e.g., azathioprine, 6-MP) are standard IBD therapies, underscoring the relevance of this MF axis.

2. **Ciliary/centrosomal module – AHI1, ALMS1, CC2D2A, C2CD3, B9D1, B9D2, CCP110**  
   - **AHI1, CC2D2A, B9D1, B9D2**: components of the transition zone at the base of primary cilia; mutations cause Joubert and Meckel syndromes.  
   - **ALMS1**: basal body protein implicated in Alström syndrome, affecting ciliary function and metabolic signaling.  
   - **C2CD3**: centriole elongation factor required for ciliogenesis.  
   - **CCP110**: centriolar protein that caps centrioles and regulates cilia assembly/disassembly.  
   These map to Reactome’s “Cilium Assembly,” “Organelle biogenesis and maintenance,” and “Cell cycle, mitotic” (via centrosome duplication).

3. **Actin cytoskeleton and membrane skeleton – CAPZ family, ANK family**  
   - **CAPZA1/2/3, CAPZB**: α/β subunits of F‑actin capping protein, which bind barbed ends of actin filaments, regulating filament length and dynamics at cell junctions and leading edges.  
   - **ANK1, ANK2, ANK3**: ankyrins that link integral membrane proteins (e.g., ion channels, adhesion molecules) to the spectrin–actin cytoskeleton, stabilizing membrane domains and junctions.  
   These genes are central to Reactome pathways like “Rho GTPase cycle,” “Regulation of actin dynamics for phagocytic cup formation,” and “Cell–cell junction organization.”

4. **Growth factor and immune–epithelial signaling – AREG**  
   - **AREG**: an EGFR ligand produced by epithelial cells, T cells, and innate lymphoid cells; promotes epithelial proliferation, mucus production, and wound healing.  
   It maps to “Signaling by EGFR,” “Signaling by ERBB2/ERBB4,” and intersects with “Cytokine signaling in immune system.”

5. **Metabolism – ADSL**  
   - **ADSL**: catalyzes two steps in de novo purine biosynthesis (conversion of SAICAR to AICAR and adenylosuccinate to AMP).  
   It maps to “Metabolism of nucleotides,” which supports high proliferative and activation demands in immune and epithelial cells during inflammation.

These functional groups are the main drivers of the Reactome pathway predictions.
reasoning.pathway_selection_rationale:
Based on the above gene clusters, the 10 most plausible Reactome pathways (at a reasonably specific level) and why they were selected are:

1. **REAC: Membrane Trafficking**  
   - Driven by ARF1/3/4/5, ARFRP1, ARFGAP1/2/3, ARCN1, BET1, BET1L, BNIP1.  
   - This high-level pathway captures the broad vesicle transport machinery that underlies secretion of cytokines, growth factors (e.g., AREG), and trafficking of receptors in intestinal epithelial and immune cells.

2. **REAC: COPI-mediated anterograde transport**  
   - Specifically supported by ARF1, ARF3, ARCN1, ARFGAP1/2/3, BET1/BET1L.  
   - Mechanistically, ARF1‑GTP recruits COPI to Golgi membranes; ARFGAPs trigger GTP hydrolysis and coat disassembly; SNAREs (BET1/BET1L) mediate vesicle fusion.  
   - This pathway is critical for proper localization of membrane proteins (e.g., transporters, adhesion molecules) in intestinal epithelium.

3. **REAC: Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport**  
   - Also driven by ARF1, ARCN1, ARFGAPs, BNIP1, BET1/BET1L.  
   - Ensures retrieval of escaped ER-resident proteins and quality control of secretory proteins; defects can cause ER stress and unfolded protein response, both implicated in IBD.

4. **REAC: Vesicle-mediated transport**  
   - A broader umbrella that includes endocytosis, exocytosis, and intra-Golgi transport, supported by the same ARF/ARFGAP/ARCN1/BET1 cluster.  
   - This is relevant for receptor internalization (e.g., EGFR, cytokine receptors) and antigen presentation in gut immune cells.

5. **REAC: Cilium Assembly**  
   - Driven by AHI1, ALMS1, CC2D2A, C2CD3, B9D1, B9D2, CCP110.  
   - Mechanistically, these proteins coordinate centriole maturation, transition zone formation, and axoneme extension.  
   - In intestinal epithelium and immune cells, primary cilia act as signaling hubs (e.g., Hedgehog, Wnt), influencing tissue patterning and immune responses.

6. **REAC: Organelle biogenesis and maintenance**  
   - Encompasses cilia, centrosomes, and other organelles; supported by the same ciliopathy genes plus centrosomal regulators.  
   - This pathway links structural organelle defects to altered signaling and cell polarity in the gut.

7. **REAC: Cell–cell junction organization**  
   - Supported by ANK1/2/3 and CAPZA1/2/3, CAPZB (via their roles in anchoring membrane proteins and regulating actin at junctions).  
   - Mechanistically, ankyrins tether adhesion molecules and channels to the spectrin–actin network, while CAPZ controls actin filament length at adherens and tight junctions.  
   - This pathway is directly relevant to epithelial barrier integrity, a central defect in IBD.

8. **REAC: Rho GTPase cycle / Regulation of actin cytoskeleton**  
   - While Rho GTPases themselves may not be in the partial list, CAPZ and ankyrins are canonical downstream effectors in actin remodeling pathways curated in Reactome.  
   - This pathway explains how external cues (e.g., cytokines, growth factors) translate into cytoskeletal changes that affect barrier function and immune cell motility.

9. **REAC: Signaling by EGFR**  
   - Driven primarily by AREG, with trafficking support from ARF/ARFGAP/ARCN1/BET1 for EGFR receptor recycling and ligand secretion.  
   - Mechanistically, AREG binding to EGFR activates downstream MAPK/PI3K pathways, promoting epithelial proliferation and repair; vesicle trafficking genes regulate receptor localization and signal duration.

10. **REAC: Metabolism of nucleotides**  
   - Driven by ADSL.  
   - While only one gene is explicitly listed here, Reactome’s nucleotide metabolism pathway is critical for rapidly dividing T cells and epithelial cells in inflamed mucosa; ADSL is a rate-limiting enzyme in purine biosynthesis, making this pathway biologically meaningful even if not statistically dominant.

These pathways are thematically connected: **vesicle trafficking and EGFR signaling** regulate epithelial repair and immune communication; **cilium/centrosome and cytoskeleton/junction pathways** regulate epithelial polarity and barrier integrity; **nucleotide metabolism** supports proliferative responses. Together, they form a coherent mechanistic framework for IBD pathogenesis.
reasoning.biological_evidence:
1. **Vesicle trafficking and ER stress in IBD**  
   - ER–Golgi trafficking defects and chronic ER stress are well-documented in IBD, particularly in Paneth cells and goblet cells, leading to impaired secretion of antimicrobial peptides and mucus.  
   - ARF1/ARCN1/ARFGAP-dependent COPI trafficking is central to maintaining ER homeostasis; perturbations can activate the unfolded protein response, which is elevated in IBD biopsies.

2. **Cilia and epithelial polarity in gut inflammation**  
   - Ciliopathy genes (e.g., AHI1, CC2D2A, ALMS1) are increasingly recognized as modulators of intestinal epithelial polarity and Wnt/Hedgehog signaling, which influence stem cell behavior and barrier function.  
   - Mouse models with ciliary defects show altered intestinal architecture and heightened susceptibility to inflammation.

3. **Barrier integrity and cytoskeleton in IBD**  
   - Disruption of tight and adherens junctions is a hallmark of IBD; actin capping proteins (CAPZ) and ankyrins are critical for junctional stability.  
   - Experimental manipulation of actin dynamics in intestinal epithelial cells alters permeability and susceptibility to colitis in animal models.

4. **EGFR/AREG in mucosal healing**  
   - AREG–EGFR signaling is protective in colitis models, promoting epithelial regeneration and mucus production; AREG is upregulated in inflamed mucosa and produced by regulatory T cells and ILC2s.  
   - Anti-TNF–resistant IBD often shows defects in mucosal healing pathways, where EGFR signaling is a key compensatory axis.

5. **Nucleotide metabolism and immune activation**  
   - Purine metabolism is essential for T cell activation and proliferation; ADSL deficiency in humans causes immune dysfunction and neurodevelopmental issues.  
   - In IBD, high proliferative turnover of immune and epithelial cells makes nucleotide metabolism a critical support pathway.

The Reactome pathways predicted here are tightly aligned with core IBD mechanisms: **epithelial barrier dysfunction**, **defective secretion and ER stress**, **altered mucosal healing via EGFR/AREG**, and **immune cell activation and proliferation**.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Dysregulated control of T cell activation can promote autoreactive T cell responses that drive CNS inflammation and demyelination in multiple sclerosis. Co‑stimulatory and inhibitory checkpoints in this pathway likely influence thresholds for pathogenic versus regulatory T cell activation in MS.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CD28 and CD2 provide key co‑stimulatory signals that enhance T cell receptor–driven activation, while CD27 supports T cell survival and differentiation, collectively tuning activation strength and persistence. CD1D shapes T cell activation by presenting lipid antigens to specialized T cell subsets, and CD274 (PD‑L1) delivers inhibitory signals that restrain excessive T cell activation.
PubMed literature synthesis: The extracellular vesicle study implicates vesicle‑mediated modulation of T cell activation and differentiation in MS, consistent with altered co‑stimulatory and inhibitory signaling in this pathway. The Mgat5 N‑glycosylation paper highlights glycan‑dependent negative regulation of T‑cell activation and autoimmunity, aligning with the role of CD28 and CD274 checkpoints, while the CD6 ligand review underscores how co‑receptor interactions at the T cell surface can be therapeutically targeted in immune‑mediated disease.
Cell/tissue context: The pathway and genes point to T cells interacting with antigen‑presenting cells in secondary lymphoid tissues and at sites of inflammation, including the CNS in multiple sclerosis, but more precise anatomical localization is not resolved from the supplied pathway‑level evidence. [PMID:28157168] [PMID:11217864] [PMID:39840036]

paragraphs: 54 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of T cell activation (GO:0050863).

Among the co-stimulatory molecules enriched in this term, CD28 functions as a prototypical activating receptor on T cells that lowers the threshold for T cell receptor signalling when engaged by its ligands. In Multiple sclerosis, genetic and functional studies implicate altered CD28-mediated co-stimulation in shaping pathogenic effector T cell responses within the central nervous system, consistent with a skewing of the balance between tolerance and autoimmunity. The ligands CD80 and CD86, expressed on antigen-presenting cells, provide the cognate signals to CD28 and thereby influence the intensity and duration of T cell activation in Multiple sclerosis lesions and peripheral immune compartments.

The inhibitory co-receptor cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA4) is a high-affinity binder of CD80 and CD86 and dampens T cell activation by competing with CD28 and recruiting inhibitory signalling machinery. Variants and functional alterations in CTLA4 have been linked to susceptibility and disease course in Multiple sclerosis, supporting a role for impaired negative regulation of T cell activation in this disease. Programmed cell death protein 1 (PDCD1) and its ligand CD274 provide an additional inhibitory axis that constrains chronically stimulated T cells, and perturbation of this pathway has been associated with exacerbation of central nervous system autoimmunity in Multiple sclerosis.

The interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain IL2RA is enriched in this pathway and forms the high-affinity receptor complex for the cytokine IL2 together with IL2RG, transducing signals via downstream kinases and transcription factors. In Multiple sclerosis, genetic variation and altered expression of IL2RA are consistently implicated in disease susceptibility and in the balance between regulatory and effector T cell populations, indicating that dysregulated IL2–IL2RA signalling contributes to defective immune tolerance. IL2 itself promotes clonal expansion and survival of activated T cells but is also crucial for regulatory T cell homeostasis, so alterations in IL2 signalling represented by IL2 and IL2RA in this pathway are highly relevant to the failure to contain autoreactive T cells in Multiple sclerosis.

Signal transducer and activator of transcription proteins STAT5A and STAT5B, which are activated downstream of IL2RA- and IL2RG-containing receptor complexes, are central transcriptional effectors of cytokine-driven T cell differentiation and survival. In the context of Multiple sclerosis, aberrant activation of a cytokine-responsive transcription factor-dependent transcriptional programmes favours the persistence of pro-inflammatory T cell subsets at the expense of regulatory populations, further linking cytokine receptor signalling in this enriched pathway to disease pathogenesis. Transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1), another key cytokine in this intersection, provides a counter-regulatory signal that can promote regulatory T cell differentiation and limit effector T cell activation, and disruptions in TGFB1-mediated regulation have been associated with heightened neuroinflammation in Multiple sclerosis.

Interleukin-6 (IL6), represented in this term together with its signalling component IL6ST, is a pleiotropic cytokine that promotes T cell activation and differentiation toward pathogenic effector phenotypes under inflammatory conditions. In Multiple sclerosis, elevated IL6 signalling has been related to enhanced T cell-driven neuroinflammation and lesion formation, aligning the enrichment of IL6 and IL6ST in this pathway with a shift toward sustained T cell activation. The common gamma-chain cytokine receptor subunit IL2RG, shared by multiple cytokine receptors, further broadens the range of cytokine inputs that can modulate T cell activation states in Multiple sclerosis.

The pan-leukocyte phosphatase PTPRC is a critical regulator of proximal T cell receptor signalling by setting the phosphorylation state of key signalling components. In Multiple sclerosis, altered function or expression of PTPRC has been associated with changes in T cell activation thresholds and signalling quality, which can favour autoreactive T cell responses. Together with non-receptor phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN2 and PTPN22 in this enriched set, PTPRC highlights the importance of phosphatase-mediated fine-tuning of T cell activation in Multiple sclerosis.

Beyond these individually highlighted proteins, the remaining intersection proteins enriched in regulation of T cell activation segregate into several functional clusters. A T cell receptor signalling machinery cluster, including CD3E, FYN, LCK, ZAP70, LAT, VAV1, RAC2, RHOH, NCK1, NCK2, SOS1, SOS2, SYK, SRC, YES1 and LYN, comprises kinases, adaptors and small GTPase regulators that propagate and shape early T cell receptor signals. A co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory surface receptor cluster, including CD1D, CD2, CD27, CD5, CD69, CD83, CD274, CD80, CD86, SLAMF1 and HAVCR2, provides additional activating or inhibitory cues that calibrate T cell activation in tissue-specific contexts relevant to Multiple sclerosis. A cytokine and growth factor signalling cluster, comprising IL2, IL2RG, IL6, IL6ST, TGFB1, EPO, IGF1, IGF2, KITLG, JAK2, JAK3, STAT5A and STAT5B, links extracellular cytokine and growth factor availability to transcriptional programmes governing T cell proliferation, survival and differentiation. Finally, a regulatory phosphatase and scaffold cluster containing PTPRC, PTPN11, PTPN2, PTPN22, LGALS3, SDC4, EFNB1, EFNB2, EFNB3 and RHOA integrates phosphatase activity with adhesion and cytoskeletal dynamics, thereby modulating the strength, duration and spatial organisation of T cell activation signals in Multiple sclerosis lesions.

Overall, enrichment of 54 Multiple sclerosis associated proteins in the term “regulation of T cell activation” underscores that dysregulated control of T cell activation is a central feature of Multiple sclerosis immunopathology. Co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory checkpoints such as CD28 and CTLA4, together with the high-affinity IL2 receptor component IL2RA, appear to drive the association by linking genetic and functional evidence for altered T cell activation thresholds directly to this pathway. Well-documented interactions within this enriched set, including binding of CD28 and CTLA4 to CD80 and CD86, engagement of PDCD1 by its ligand CD274, and signalling from IL2 through IL2RA–IL2RG to STAT5A and STAT5B, illustrate how coordinated perturbations across receptors, ligands and downstream signalling modules can converge to sustain pathogenic T cell responses in Multiple sclerosis. These findings support the view that therapeutic strategies targeting the regulation of T cell activation at multiple levels may be particularly effective in modifying disease activity in Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: Exactly 41 Multiple sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO:BP pathway “positive regulation of T cell activation” (GO:0050870).

Among the proximal T cell receptor signaling molecules enriched in this term, PTPN22, LCK and ZAP70 stand out as key regulators of T cell activation thresholds. PTPN22 encodes a lymphoid protein tyrosine phosphatase that constrains antigen receptor signaling, and genetic variation in PTPN22 has been repeatedly linked to altered T cell reactivity in Multiple sclerosis, consistent with a role in skewing the balance toward pathogenic activation. LCK, a Src family kinase, and the ζ‑chain–associated kinase ZAP70 form a critical tandem at the T cell receptor complex, where LCK-mediated phosphorylation events enable ZAP70 activation; perturbations in this axis have been implicated in abnormal T cell signaling profiles described in Multiple sclerosis, supporting their contribution to excessive or dysregulated positive regulation of T cell activation in the disease context.

A second group of notable proteins comprises HAVCR2, SLAMF1 and TGFB1, which modulate the quality and persistence of T cell activation in inflammatory settings. HAVCR2 functions as an inhibitory receptor on T cells that is often upregulated in chronically stimulated lymphocytes, and altered HAVCR2 expression patterns have been reported in Multiple sclerosis, suggesting maladapted attempts to restrain ongoing T cell activation. SLAMF1, an immunoglobulin superfamily receptor involved in co-stimulatory signaling, is expressed on activated T cells and has been found upregulated in Multiple sclerosis lesions, consistent with its participation in sustaining pathogenic T cell responses within the central nervous system. TGFB1, a pleiotropic cytokine with well-established roles in T cell differentiation and activation control, shows genetic and expression-level alterations in Multiple sclerosis that are compatible with disturbed regulatory circuits governing the intensity and duration of T cell activation.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional clusters centered on co-stimulation, cytokine and growth factor signaling, and intracellular signal transduction. A co-stimulatory and antigen-recognition cluster includes CD1D, CD27, CD28, CD3E, CD5, CD80, CD83, CD86, CD274, SLAMF1 and HAVCR2, which collectively provide additional signals beyond T cell receptor ligation to enhance or shape T cell activation, and several of these molecules have been implicated in Multiple sclerosis through altered expression on peripheral or lesional T cells and antigen-presenting cells. A cytokine and growth factor cluster, incorporating IL2, IL2RA, IL2RG, IL6, IL6ST, EPO, IGF1, IGF2, KITLG and TGFB1, supports the expansion, survival and differentiation of activated T cells through receptor-mediated positive regulation of activation programs, and dysregulation of these pathways has been observed in Multiple sclerosis immune compartments. Finally, an intracellular signaling and cytoskeletal-remodeling cluster, including FYN, LYN, SRC, YES1, SYK, VAV1, JAK2, STAT5B, PTPN11, NCK1, NCK2, RHOA, RHOH and PTPRC, integrates signals from the T cell receptor, co-stimulatory receptors and cytokine receptors to propagate and stabilize activation, with several members reported to show altered activation states or expression in Multiple sclerosis T cells, consistent with globally enhanced positive regulation of T cell activation.

Taken together, enrichment of these proteins in “positive regulation of T cell activation” underscores that a core feature of the Multiple sclerosis gene module is the reinforcement of signaling pathways that drive and sustain T cell activation. The association appears to be driven particularly by proximal T cell receptor regulators such as PTPN22, LCK and ZAP70, whose combined disruption can substantially alter activation thresholds. Well-documented interactions among the proteins listed for this record, including the functional pairing of LCK and ZAP70 at the T cell receptor complex and the engagement of CD28 by its co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86, highlight that multiple, physically connected signaling nodes are concurrently represented. This convergence supports the interpretation that the Multiple sclerosis module is enriched for an interconnected network of molecules that together amplify the positive regulation of T cell activation.
