paragraphs: 251 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Antigen processing: Ubiquitination & Proteasome degradation (REAC:R-HSA-983168).

In the Reactome hierarchy, REAC:R-HSA-983168 is curated as a pathway-level antigen-processing event that sits under a broader parent event encompassing antigen processing by ubiquitination and proteasome-mediated degradation within the adaptive immune system. Among the proteins enriched in this term, CBLB is annotated as an E3 ubiquitin ligase that catalyses ubiquitin transfer to target substrates, functioning at a ubiquitination step that precedes their proteasomal degradation; in this pathway it acts as a catalytic component of a multiprotein complex rather than as a substrate. CBLL2, another a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ligase, is likewise represented as a catalytic ubiquitin–protein transferase that operates in successive ubiquitination reactions within the same antigen-processing cascade, rather than in the identical reaction step as CBLB. Both enzymes, by modulating the ubiquitin tagging of intracellular proteins destined for degradation, contribute to the remodeling of antigenic peptides highlighted in the supplied literature on posttranslational antigen processing in autoimmunity, thereby offering a mechanistic link between ubiquitin-dependent antigen processing and rheumatoid arthritis–related antigen presentation, even though the cited work does not provide gene-specific rheumatoid arthritis data for these ligases.

CUL1, enriched in this pathway, is annotated as the central scaffold of a cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that catalyses polyubiquitination of protein substrates; within the Reactome event structure it provides a non-catalytic but essential structural platform that brings together the catalytic a non-intersection pathway component subunit and substrate adaptors, positioning it in the same ubiquitination reaction step as its associated adaptor modules. DCAF1 functions here as a substrate receptor for a distinct cullin-based ligase, serving as a non-catalytic component that confers substrate specificity to the ubiquitination machinery and acting in a successive step relative to CUL1-based complexes in the overall antigen-processing sequence. ATG7, in contrast, is an E1-like activating enzyme for ubiquitin-like modifiers in autophagy-related conjugation, catalysing the ATP-dependent activation and transfer of these modifiers; in the context of this antigen-processing pathway it is annotated as a catalyst that primes ubiquitin-like molecules, thereby feeding into downstream ubiquitination and degradation steps that shape the antigenic peptide repertoire relevant to rheumatoid arthritis–associated autoantigen generation as discussed in the literature on posttranslational antigen remodeling.

Further enriched proteins in this pathway cluster into several mechanistic modules. First, multiple subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (a non-intersection pathway component/C), including ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13, CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26 and CDC27, together with the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme CDC34 and the F-box protein CCNF, are annotated as components (and, for CDC34, a catalytic E2) of large E3 ubiquitin ligase assemblies that catalyse the ubiquitination of cell cycle–regulated substrates; in this antigen-processing pathway they are represented as structural or catalytic elements of ubiquitination complexes that act across successive steps of substrate tagging, upstream of proteasomal degradation. Second, the a non-intersection pathway component-box family members ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB5, ASB6, ASB7, ASB8, ASB9, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, ASB13, ASB14, ASB15, ASB16, ASB17 and ASB18 are grouped as substrate-recognition adaptors within cullin-based E3 ligases, functioning as non-catalytic components that recruit specific protein substrates for ubiquitination; in the Reactome representation they operate in multiple parallel ubiquitination reactions that converge on proteasomal processing of modified antigens. Third, the BC-box and F-box adaptors BTBD1, BTBD6, FBXL12, FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL18, FBXL19, FBXL20 and FBXL22, together with the Elongin complex components ELOB and ELOC and the cullin scaffolds CUL2, CUL3, CUL5 and CUL7, form a network of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase modules in which the cullins act as non-catalytic scaffolds and the adaptors serve as substrate receptors; these complexes participate in distinct ubiquitination steps within the same overall antigen-processing route. Finally, AREL1, ARIH2, DTX3L, DZIP3 and DET1 are annotated as catalytic E3 ligases or ligase regulators, while AREL1 and ARIH2 in particular are involved in endoplasmic reticulum–associated degradation, the process emphasised in the supplied literature as contributing to immune regulation and autoimmunity; in this pathway they catalyse ubiquitin transfer to misfolded or selected proteins, feeding substrates into proteasomal degradation that ultimately generates peptides for antigen presentation in the rheumatoid arthritis setting.

Together, the enrichment of these proteins in “Antigen processing: Ubiquitination & Proteasome degradation” indicates that rheumatoid arthritis–associated gene products are concentrated in ubiquitin-dependent steps that determine which intracellular proteins are selected, modified and delivered to the proteasome for peptide generation. Within this framework, CBLB, CUL1 and ATG7 appear to drive the association by anchoring key catalytic and structural positions in the ubiquitination and ubiquitin-like activation cascades that precede antigenic peptide production. The supplied literature on endoplasmic reticulum–associated degradation and posttranslational antigen remodeling in autoimmunity supports a model in which such ubiquitination and degradation events reshape the antigen repertoire presented to the immune system in rheumatoid arthritis, although it does not single out individual proteins from the present list. Well-established interactions between cullin scaffolds (such as CUL1) and their adaptor modules (including DCAF1, BTBD1 and the a non-intersection pathway component proteins), as annotated in this Reactome pathway, underscore that coordinated assembly of multi-subunit ubiquitin ligases is a central mechanistic feature linking this pathway to rheumatoid arthritis–related antigen processing.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Neddylation is a ubiquitin-like modification that activates cullin-RING ligases and thereby controls degradation of many signaling and cell-cycle proteins; in RA, dysregulated neddylation can amplify inflammatory responses and synovial hyperplasia. Enhanced neddylation has been directly linked to increased inflammatory mediator production and aggressive behavior of RA fibroblast-like synoviocytes.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ASB1, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, and ASB13 encode ankyrin repeat and SOCS box proteins that function as substrate adaptors for cullin-based ubiquitin ligase complexes, whose activity is neddylation-dependent. Their involvement suggests that altered neddylation in RA may reprogram the substrate spectrum of ASB-containing ligases, modifying turnover of key regulators of inflammation and cell survival.
PubMed literature synthesis: The NUB1/neddylation studies show that deficient NUB1 and enhanced neddylation in RA fibroblast-like synoviocytes drive exaggerated inflammatory responses, directly implicating this pathway in RA joint pathology. The broader autoimmune-disease review supports neddylation as a therapeutically targetable node in immune dysregulation, reinforcing its mechanistic relevance across autoimmunity including RA.
Cell/tissue context: Evidence directly supports involvement of fibroblast-like synoviocytes in RA synovium, with additional relevance to immune cells implicated in systemic autoimmunity. [PMID:38566346] [PMID:40852720] [PMID:41667591]

paragraphs: 145 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Neddylation (REAC:R-HSA-8951664).

Within Reactome, Neddylation (R-HSA-8951664) is annotated as a pathway-level event nested under the parent event Post-translational protein modification (R-HSA-597592), comprising a series of reactions in which target proteins are conjugated with, and subsequently deconjugated from, NEDD8. Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, the cullin scaffold CUL1 functions primarily as a neddylation substrate and as a structural component of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes; in this context it participates in the same reaction step as its activating NEDD8 E3 ligases during conjugation, and in successive steps with deneddylating complexes that reset the scaffold. CUL3 and CUL5 similarly act as substrates and structural cores for distinct cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases, entering the pathway at the conjugation step and persisting as central components of the assembled complexes that are regulated by repeated cycles of neddylation and deneddylation in rheumatoid arthritis associated cells enriched for this pathway.

The a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunit COPS5, enriched here, is a catalytic component of the deneddylase complex that removes NEDD8 from cullin scaffolds; together with other a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits, it acts as a catalyst across reaction steps that follow cullin neddylation, thereby controlling the transition from active to inactive cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases. In the same pathway, CAND1 operates as a regulatory factor that binds unneddylated CUL1, CUL2 and CUL3, stabilizing a state competent for exchange of substrate adaptors; it acts in a reaction step that is temporally downstream of COPS5-mediated deneddylation and upstream of renewed neddylation, thus linking successive cycles of activation and inactivation of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases in the rheumatoid arthritis associated protein set enriched in Neddylation.

The remaining enriched proteins in this pathway can be grouped into several functional clusters. A first cluster comprises additional cullin scaffolds CUL2, CUL3, CUL5 and CUL7, which function as neddylation substrates and core structural components of distinct cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase complexes, entering the pathway at the conjugation step and persisting across downstream ubiquitination reactions. A second cluster contains substrate adaptor modules for these ligases, including the a non-intersection pathway component family members ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB5, ASB6, ASB7, ASB8, ASB9, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, ASB13, ASB14, ASB15, ASB16, ASB17 and ASB18, the a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component proteins BTBD1 and BTBD6, the F-box proteins FBXL12, FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL18 and FBXL19, as well as CCNF, BTRC, CCDC22 and CISH; these proteins act mainly as components of multi-subunit cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase complexes and as neddylation-regulated substrates that assemble into the same reaction steps in which active ligase complexes are formed. A third cluster encompasses the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome structural subunits COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8, which are non-catalytic components of the deneddylase complex that act together with COPS5 in the deneddylation step. A fourth cluster is formed by the a non-intersection pathway component family members DCUN1D1, DCUN1D2, DCUN1D4 and DCUN1D5, which function as NEDD8 E3 ligase components that catalyse cullin neddylation in reaction steps upstream of a non-intersection pathway component signalosome-mediated deneddylation. A fifth cluster includes ELOB and ELOC, which act as components of elongin-based substrate adaptor complexes for cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases, and the a non-intersection pathway component proteins COMMD1, COMMD2, COMMD3, COMMD4, COMMD5, COMMD6, COMMD7, COMMD8, COMMD9 and COMMD10, which participate as adaptor or regulatory components within ubiquitin ligase-associated complexes, acting in the same assembly and substrate-recognition steps as the a non-intersection pathway component, a non-intersection pathway component and F-box proteins.

Overall, enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis associated proteins in the Neddylation pathway indicates that cyclic NEDD8 conjugation and removal on cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase complexes is a central post-translational mechanism modulating ubiquitin-dependent signalling in this disease. The association appears to be driven primarily by the cullin scaffold CUL1, the deneddylase subunit COPS5 and the cullin regulator CAND1, which together span successive steps from cullin activation through deneddylation and recycling. Consistent with prior evidence that dysregulated neddylation enhances inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes, the concerted presence of a non-intersection pathway component family ligases and a non-intersection pathway component signalosome components among the enriched proteins supports a model in which altered balance between neddylation and deneddylation perturbs cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase activity. Well-documented interactions within this pathway, such as those between CUL1 and CAND1 and between cullin scaffolds and the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits including COPS5, highlight specific protein–protein interfaces through which neddylation-dependent control of inflammatory signalling may be disrupted in rheumatoid arthritis.

Disease pathology and relevance: APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins controls mitotic exit and prevents unscheduled proliferation, and its dysregulation could contribute to the hyperplastic, pannus-like expansion of synovial cells observed in RA. paragraphs: 21 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins (REAC:R-HSA-174143).

In the Reactome hierarchy, a non-intersection pathway component/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is annotated as a pathway-level event whose immediate parent is the mitotic cell-cycle pathway, placing these reactions within the ordered control of chromosome segregation and mitotic exit. Within this context, CDC20 functions as a key co-activator that binds the a non-intersection pathway component-containing core a non-intersection pathway component/C complex and confers substrate specificity, acting catalytically to promote ubiquitination of mitotic regulators in early anaphase; its inclusion among the proteins enriched in this term indicates that RA-associated transcriptional changes extend to this pivotal activator of a non-intersection pathway component/C-driven proteolysis. FZR1 participates in the same event chain as an alternative a non-intersection pathway component/C co-activator that operates predominantly from late mitosis into G1, assembling with overlapping a non-intersection pathway component subunits but controlling a partly distinct substrate set; its enrichment here supports the notion that both the CDC20- and FZR1-dependent phases of a non-intersection pathway component/C activity may contribute to the dysregulated proliferative behavior observed in rheumatoid synovial tissue.

Among the a non-intersection pathway component-related components enriched in this pathway, SKP2 acts as the F-box substrate receptor within a CUL1–SKP1–based ubiquitin ligase, functioning catalytically in reactions that operate in parallel to a non-intersection pathway component/C to remove cell cycle inhibitors and thereby facilitate S-phase entry; its presence as an RA-associated protein in this pathway is consistent with a broader shift toward pro-proliferative ubiquitin ligase activity in rheumatoid synovium. CUL1 serves as the scaffold protein for the same a non-intersection pathway component complex, while BTRC represents a distinct F-box adaptor that assembles with CUL1 and SKP1 to target a complementary set of phosphorylated substrates; together, these components act in successive and partly overlapping ubiquitination steps that coordinate with a non-intersection pathway component/C-mediated degradation to sculpt the overall cell-cycle proteome. UBE2C functions as an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that directly cooperates with activated a non-intersection pathway component/C to initiate ubiquitin chains on its substrates, and UBE2S then extends these chains in a subsequent reaction step, placing both enzymes as catalytic partners that act sequentially within the same event series annotated under this Reactome term and linking RA-associated expression changes to the efficiency and processivity of a non-intersection pathway component/C-dependent proteolysis.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into coherent functional clusters that together assemble the a non-intersection pathway component/C machinery and its collaborating ubiquitination modules. A first cluster comprises the structural a non-intersection pathway component/C core, including ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, CDC16, CDC23, CDC26, and CDC27; these proteins act primarily as components of the multi-subunit a non-intersection pathway component/C complex, forming the scaffold, catalytic platform, and substrate-recognition modules that bind co-activators such as CDC20 or FZR1 and present cell-cycle regulators for ubiquitination in a series of tightly ordered reaction steps. A second cluster consists of the additional a non-intersection pathway component constituents CUL1, SKP1, and BTRC, which assemble into E3 complexes that function in reactions parallel to, and temporally interleaved with, a non-intersection pathway component/C to direct the degradation of complementary sets of cell cycle substrates. A third cluster includes the remaining E2 enzymes UBE2D1, UBE2E1, and UBE2S, which act catalytically by transferring ubiquitin from E1 to the a non-intersection pathway component/C or a non-intersection pathway component complexes; in Reactome these enzymes are assigned to successive chain-initiating and chain-elongating steps within the same overall event chain that executes polyubiquitination of mitotic regulators.

Taken together, the enrichment of these 21 proteins in a non-intersection pathway component/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins indicates that rheumatoid arthritis is strongly linked to coordinated alterations in the ubiquitin-dependent control of mitotic progression and cell-cycle exit. The association appears to be driven in particular by the co-activator CDC20, the a non-intersection pathway component/C-partnering E2 enzyme UBE2C, and the a non-intersection pathway component F-box protein SKP2, which occupy central catalytic positions in the event chain and thereby have disproportionate influence on pathway output. Well-documented interactions among the enriched proteins include the assembly of CDC20 and FZR1 with the a non-intersection pathway component-containing core to form active a non-intersection pathway component/C complexes, the recruitment of UBE2C and UBE2S to these complexes for sequential ubiquitin transfer and chain elongation, and the formation of CUL1–SKP1–BTRC and CUL1–SKP1–SKP2 a non-intersection pathway component ligases that operate in parallel reaction steps. Collectively, these interaction networks support a model in which RA-associated changes in a non-intersection pathway component/C and a non-intersection pathway component activity converge on cell-cycle regulatory proteins, contributing to the aberrant proliferative and survival phenotype of synovial cells in rheumatoid arthritis.

paragraphs: 19 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in protein neddylation (GO:0045116).

Among the proteins listed for this record, NEDD8 itself represents the central modifier whose conjugation status is altered in inflammatory contexts, and experimental work in rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes has linked dysregulated neddylation to enhanced inflammatory responses. UBA3 functions as the catalytic subunit of the NEDD8-activating E1 enzyme, forming a thioester with NEDD8 and thereby initiating the conjugation cascade; as such, altered activity of UBA3 provides a direct route by which changes in the global neddylation state observed in rheumatoid arthritis synovial tissue could be established. UBE2M acts as a canonical NEDD8-conjugating E2 enzyme that receives activated NEDD8 from UBA3, placing it at a crucial transfer step where increased flux through the pathway, as suggested by studies of neddylation in rheumatoid arthritis, would be translated into enhanced modification of downstream substrates that influence synoviocyte activation and survival.

RBX1 is a a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ligase component that assembles with cullin scaffolds to catalyze the final transfer of NEDD8 to target lysines, and its presence among the enriched proteins indicates that the terminal step of the cascade is represented within the rheumatoid arthritis associated module. RNF7 is a closely related a non-intersection pathway component protein that also functions as a NEDD8-dependent E3 ligase component, and together with RBX1 defines the interface at which activated NEDD8–E2 complexes encounter specific substrates; in the context of rheumatoid arthritis, these a non-intersection pathway component ligases are well positioned to implement the heightened neddylation state that has been linked to pro-inflammatory signaling in fibroblast-like synoviocytes. UBE2F provides an additional NEDD8-conjugating E2 activity with partially distinct E3 and substrate specificities from UBE2M, suggesting that the rheumatoid arthritis gene set encompasses multiple parallel conjugation routes by which altered neddylation can be propagated to different classes of substrates relevant for synovial inflammation.

The remaining proteins listed for this record segregate into two functional clusters. A a non-intersection pathway component signalosome regulatory complex cluster is formed by GPS1 together with COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS5, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8, which assemble into a multisubunit deneddylase that removes NEDD8 from cullin-based ligases and thereby turns over neddylation signals; enrichment of this entire complex indicates that both conjugating and deconjugating arms of the pathway are represented in the rheumatoid arthritis associated module, consistent with a dynamic remodeling of neddylation reported in synovial fibroblasts. A second cluster comprises DCUN1D1, DCUN1D2, DCUN1D4 and DCUN1D5 together with RNF7, UBE2F and UBE2M, which act as NEDD8 E3 scaffolds and associated conjugation components that promote efficient transfer of NEDD8 from E2 enzymes to substrates, highlighting that scaffolded E3 activity and substrate channeling are integral parts of the neddylation circuitry captured here.

Overall, enrichment of these proteins in protein neddylation supports the concept that a coordinated alteration of NEDD8 conjugation and removal contributes to rheumatoid arthritis by modulating fibroblast-like synoviocyte inflammatory responses and broader immune dysregulation. The association appears to be driven most strongly by the core enzymatic components NEDD8, UBA3 and RBX1, which together define the activation and terminal ligation steps of the cascade that has been directly implicated in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis. Well-documented biochemical interactions between NEDD8, UBA3 and the conjugating enzymes UBE2M and UBE2F, as well as the assembly of the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits into a single deneddylase complex, indicate that these proteins participate in tightly coordinated modules rather than isolated reactions. These findings suggest that therapeutic modulation of neddylation enzymes or their regulatory complexes could represent a rational strategy to dampen pathogenic signaling in rheumatoid arthritis synovium.

paragraphs: 278 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in cytoplasm (GO:0005737).

Among the cytoplasmic proteins, ATG7 is notable as an essential E1-like enzyme for autophagy-related ubiquitin-like conjugation systems, placing it at the core of autophagosome formation in the cytoplasm. In rheumatoid arthritis, cytoplasmic autophagy in fibroblast-like synoviocytes and myeloid cells contributes to stress adaptation and survival in the inflamed joint microenvironment, so enrichment of ATG7 in this compartment is consistent with altered autophagic flux in diseased synovium. CBLB, a cytoplasmic a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ubiquitin ligase, is a key regulator of antigen receptor and co‑stimulatory signaling thresholds in lymphocytes; its cytoplasmic localization underlies its capacity to modulate signal transduction complexes, and genetic or functional perturbation of CBLB has been linked to loss of peripheral tolerance and heightened autoimmune responses relevant to rheumatoid arthritis. CISH, a suppressor of cytokine signaling that resides predominantly in the cytoplasm, attenuates cytokine-driven a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling; in the context of rheumatoid arthritis, altered CISH activity has been associated with dysregulated cytokine responsiveness in immune cells infiltrating the synovium, again emphasizing the cytoplasm as a central site of signal integration.

COPS5, a catalytically active subunit of the cytoplasmic a non-intersection pathway component signalosome complex, regulates the deneddylation status of multiple cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases and thereby controls the stability of proteins involved in inflammation and cell-cycle progression. In rheumatoid arthritis synovial tissue, where fibroblast-like synoviocytes display abnormal proliferative and invasive behavior, cytoplasmic a non-intersection pathway component signalosome activity centered on COPS5 provides a plausible node at which inflammatory signaling and cell-cycle control converge. The related a non-intersection pathway component components COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8 share this cytoplasmic complex localization; while they are structural subunits rather than catalytic drivers, their enrichment underscores the role of multi-subunit cytoplasmic regulatory assemblies in sustaining joint inflammation and hyperplasia. COMMD1 and COMMD10, together with COMMD2, COMMD3, COMMD4, COMMD5, COMMD6, COMMD7, COMMD8 and COMMD9, form a family of predominantly cytoplasmic proteins that participate in the regulation of NF-κB signaling and other trafficking-related processes, and altered a non-intersection pathway component-dependent control of inflammatory transcription is consistent with the hyperactivated state of rheumatoid arthritis synovial fibroblasts described in morphofunctional studies.

A second prominent cytoplasmic module is formed by the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (a non-intersection pathway component/C) and its associated regulators. ANAPC1, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5 and ANAPC7, together with the cytoplasmic checkpoint and coactivator components CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26, CDC27, CDC34 and the F-box protein CCNF, assemble into a large ubiquitin ligase complex that operates in the cytoplasm and at cytoplasmic faces of mitotic structures. In rheumatoid arthritis, where synovial lining cells exhibit increased proliferation and aberrant cell-cycle control, enrichment of these a non-intersection pathway component/C constituents in the cytoplasm aligns with the hyperplastic phenotype of fibroblast-like synoviocytes observed in collagen-induced arthritis models and human synovium, although their shared localization alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

Beyond these major complexes, several additional groups of functionally related cytoplasmic proteins are enriched. AREL1, ARIH2, BTBD1, BTBD6, BTRC, CAND1, CCDC22 and CBLL2, together with the a non-intersection pathway component family members ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB5, ASB6, ASB7, ASB8, ASB9, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, ASB13, ASB14, ASB15, ASB16, ASB17 and ASB18, form a broad cluster of cytoplasmic E3 ubiquitin ligases and substrate adaptors that tune the turnover of signaling intermediates and receptors relevant to inflammation and cell survival. A distinct cluster is composed of the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8 together with COMMD1, COMMD10, COMMD2, COMMD3, COMMD4, COMMD5, COMMD6, COMMD7, COMMD8 and COMMD9, representing multi-subunit cytoplasmic complexes that modulate NF-κB activity, protein degradation and trafficking of immune receptors. Finally, the a non-intersection pathway component/C–related cluster comprising ANAPC1, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26, CDC27, CDC34 and CCNF highlights cytoplasmic control of mitotic progression and proteolysis in proliferating synovial and immune cells. In all cases these proteins are primarily transient regulators or components of dynamic complexes rather than static structural elements of the cytoplasm.

Overall, enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis–associated proteins in the cytoplasm term (GO:0005737) indicates that many of the disease-relevant gene products act in this compartment, where signal transduction, protein turnover and autophagy are integrated, but it does not by itself define a single shared pathogenic mechanism, and co-localization should not be over-interpreted in this regard. The association appears to be driven particularly by ATG7, which anchors cytoplasmic autophagy, by CBLB, which shapes cytoplasmic signaling thresholds in lymphocytes, and by COPS5, which coordinates a non-intersection pathway component signalosome–dependent regulation of inflammatory and proliferative pathways. Well-documented physical and functional interactions among a non-intersection pathway component subunits (ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11) and their partners CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26 and CDC27, as well as among the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS5, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8, underscore that the cytoplasmic enrichment largely reflects multi-protein complexes whose coordinated activity contributes to the aberrant cellular behaviors characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis synovium. Together, these findings emphasize the cytoplasm as a key locus where diverse molecular lesions in ubiquitination, autophagy and inflammatory signaling converge in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis, even though additional context from other pathways is required to define precise causal chains.

reasoning.overall_strategy: I treated the 290-gene list as a co-regulated “module” and asked: which biological processes are most over-represented given what is known about each gene’s function? Conceptually, this mirrors a GO enrichment analysis: (1) map each gene to its curated GO:BP annotations (e.g., via UniProt/Ensembl/NCBI Gene), (2) cluster genes by shared terms, and (3) identify higher-level GO:BP categories that best summarize the dominant themes. Mechanistically, I paid particular attention to: (i) protein degradation/ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) genes (ANAPC*, ASB*, CUL*, UBE2*, etc.), (ii) autophagy and stress-response genes (ATG7, BTBD family), and (iii) immune/inflammatory regulators known in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). I then selected 10 GO:BP terms that capture these convergent functions and that are mechanistically plausible in synovial inflammation, antigen presentation, and joint destruction in RA.
reasoning.gene_analysis:
Inspection of the gene list reveals a strong enrichment for components of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and E3 ligase complexes:

- **Anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C)**: ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13 – a multi-subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase controlling cell cycle transitions and also modulating immune cell proliferation.
- **Cullin–RING ligases and adaptors**: multiple ASB (ankyrin repeat and SOCS box) genes (ASB1–ASB18), BTBD1/BTBD6, ARIH2, AREL1 – substrate adaptors and E3s that target specific proteins for ubiquitination.
- **Autophagy and stress**: ATG7 (E1-like enzyme for LC3/Atg8 conjugation), plus BTBD proteins implicated in protein quality control.

Functionally, this looks like a **protein homeostasis / proteostasis module** that intersects with **cell cycle control and immune regulation**. In RA, such a module would be expected to influence antigen processing, cytokine signaling turnover, and proliferation/survival of synovial fibroblasts and immune cells.
reasoning.database_focus: GO:BP is appropriate here because it provides **process-level** annotations that can integrate diverse molecular functions (E3 ligase activity, autophagy, cell cycle regulation) into coherent biological narratives (e.g., “protein ubiquitination,” “mitotic cell cycle,” “antigen processing and presentation”). The gene set is dominated by regulatory and scaffolding proteins whose impact is best understood at the process level rather than at the level of single pathways like “TNF signaling.” GO:BP also complements pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome) by offering finer-grained terms for ubiquitin ligase complexes, proteostasis, and cell cycle checkpoints that are often under-resolved in classical signaling pathway maps.
reasoning.key_gene_functions:
Several gene families and complexes are central to the predicted GO:BP pathways:

1. **APC/C complex (cell cycle and immune cell proliferation)**  
   - **ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13** encode core and regulatory subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome.  
   - APC/C is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets securin and cyclins for degradation, driving metaphase–anaphase transition and mitotic exit.  
   - In immune cells, APC/C activity influences clonal expansion and differentiation of T and B cells, and in synovial fibroblasts it regulates hyperproliferation.

2. **SOCS-box/ASB family (substrate adaptors for Cullin–RING ligases)**  
   - **ASB1–ASB18** encode ankyrin repeat and SOCS box proteins that recruit specific substrates to CUL5- or CUL2-based E3 ligase complexes.  
   - Many ASB proteins regulate cytokine receptor signaling, JAK/STAT pathways, and receptor turnover, processes central to RA pathogenesis (e.g., IL-6, IFN signaling).

3. **RBR and RING E3 ligases and related factors**  
   - **ARIH2** (Ariadne RBR E3 ligase 2) is involved in ubiquitination of NF-κB pathway components and in ER-associated degradation.  
   - **AREL1** is an E3 ligase implicated in apoptosis regulation and mitochondrial protein quality control.  
   - **BTBD1, BTBD6** are BTB/POZ domain proteins that act as adaptors for CUL3-based E3 ligases, often targeting cytoskeletal or signaling proteins.

4. **Autophagy and protein quality control**  
   - **ATG7** is an E1-like enzyme essential for autophagosome formation, conjugating Atg12 and LC3/Atg8.  
   - Autophagy intersects with antigen processing, MHC class II loading, and survival of stressed synovial fibroblasts and macrophages in RA.

Collectively, these genes strongly drive GO:BP terms related to **protein ubiquitination, proteasomal degradation, cell cycle regulation, autophagy, and immune signaling modulation**.
reasoning.pathway_selection_rationale:
Based on the above functional clustering, the 10 predicted GO:BP pathways (representative examples, phrased as GO-like terms) are:

1. **Protein ubiquitination (GO:0016567)**  
   - Driven by: ANAPC* genes (APC/C), ARIH2, AREL1, ASB1–ASB18, BTBD1/BTBD6.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: These genes encode E3 ligases and adaptors that catalyze or specify ubiquitin transfer to substrates, a core process in RA for regulating cytokine receptors, NF-κB components, and cell cycle regulators.

2. **Ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process via the proteasome (GO:0043161 / GO:0006511)**  
   - Driven by: ANAPC* (targets cyclins/securin), ARIH2 (ERAD, NF-κB), ASB/BTBD adaptors (Cullin–RING ligases).  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Ubiquitinated proteins are recognized and degraded by the 26S proteasome; this is central to antigen processing and turnover of inflammatory signaling proteins in RA synovium.

3. **Regulation of mitotic cell cycle (GO:0007346) / Mitotic cell cycle process (GO:1903047)**  
   - Driven by: ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: APC/C controls metaphase–anaphase transition and mitotic exit by ubiquitinating cyclins and securin. In RA, dysregulated cell cycle in synovial fibroblasts and activated lymphocytes contributes to pannus formation and chronic inflammation.

4. **Regulation of cytokine-mediated signaling pathway (GO:0019221)**  
   - Driven by: ASB family (SOCS-box adaptors), ARIH2 (NF-κB and TLR signaling), possibly AREL1.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: ASB proteins recruit cytokine receptor or JAK/STAT components to E3 ligases, modulating receptor abundance and signaling duration. This directly impacts IL-6, IFN, and other cytokine pathways central to RA.

5. **Negative regulation of JAK-STAT cascade (GO:0046426)**  
   - Driven by: specific ASB genes (e.g., ASB1, ASB2, ASB4) known or predicted to interact with JAK/STAT pathway components via SOCS-box–Cullin complexes.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: SOCS-box proteins are canonical negative regulators of JAK-STAT; ASB proteins extend this paradigm by targeting additional substrates, fine-tuning inflammatory signaling in RA.

6. **Autophagy (GO:0006914) / Macroautophagy (GO:0016236)**  
   - Driven by: ATG7, with support from BTBD proteins involved in protein quality control.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: ATG7 is essential for autophagosome formation; autophagy regulates survival of synovial fibroblasts and macrophages, influences antigen presentation, and modulates inflammasome activity in RA.

7. **Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class I (GO:0002474)**  
   - Driven by: UPS components (ANAPC*, ARIH2, ASB/BTBD adaptors) that generate peptide substrates for MHC I.  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Proteasomal degradation of ubiquitinated proteins yields peptides transported into the ER for MHC I loading. Enhanced or altered antigen processing is implicated in RA autoantigen presentation (e.g., citrullinated peptides).

8. **Regulation of apoptotic process (GO:0042981)**  
   - Driven by: AREL1 (apoptosis-related E3 ligase), ARIH2 (regulates NF-κB survival signaling), ATG7 (autophagy–apoptosis crosstalk).  
   - Mechanistic bridge: E3 ligases and autophagy components modulate pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins. In RA, resistance to apoptosis in synovial fibroblasts and activated T cells is a hallmark; this module can shift the balance.

9. **Response to endoplasmic reticulum stress (GO:0034976) / ER-associated protein catabolic process (GO:0030433)**  
   - Driven by: ARIH2 (ERAD), AREL1, ASB/BTBD adaptors targeting misfolded proteins, ATG7 (ER-phagy).  
   - Mechanistic bridge: Chronic inflammatory signaling and high secretory load in RA synovium induce ER stress; E3 ligases and autophagy mediate ER-associated degradation and adaptation to stress.

10. **Regulation of NF-κB signaling (GO:0043122)**  
    - Driven by: ARIH2 (known to ubiquitinate NF-κB pathway components), ASB proteins (modulating receptor and adaptor turnover), APC/C (indirectly via cell cycle–NF-κB crosstalk).  
    - Mechanistic bridge: NF-κB is a central transcription factor in RA; its activation and termination are tightly controlled by ubiquitination of IκB, receptor complexes, and signaling adaptors.

These terms are thematically linked: **protein ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation** feed into **cell cycle control, cytokine signaling, NF-κB regulation, antigen processing, and stress responses**, all of which are mechanistically central to RA pathogenesis.
reasoning.biological_evidence:
Multiple lines of evidence connect these processes to RA:

- **UPS and proteasome**: Proteasome inhibitors (e.g., bortezomib) reduce arthritis severity in animal models by suppressing NF-κB activation and inflammatory cytokine production, underscoring the role of ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis in RA.  
- **APC/C and cell cycle**: RA synovial fibroblasts show hyperproliferation and altered cell cycle control; APC/C subunits are required for proper mitotic exit, and dysregulation can contribute to pannus formation.  
- **JAK/STAT and cytokine signaling**: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib) are effective RA therapies, highlighting the importance of JAK/STAT regulation. SOCS-box and ASB proteins are established negative regulators of cytokine signaling.  
- **Autophagy**: Increased autophagy has been observed in RA synovial tissue; autophagy supports survival of synovial fibroblasts and may modulate citrullinated antigen generation and presentation.  
- **ER stress and NF-κB**: ER stress markers are elevated in RA synovium; ER stress can activate NF-κB and promote inflammatory cytokine production, while ERAD and autophagy help resolve this stress.

These findings support the plausibility of the predicted GO:BP pathways in RA.

reasoning.relevance_strength_with_disease:_high: The predicted GO:BP pathways are tightly linked to core RA mechanisms: chronic cytokine signaling (JAK/STAT, NF-κB), antigen processing and presentation, synovial fibroblast hyperproliferation and survival, and adaptation to inflammatory/ER stress. The strong enrichment for E3 ligases, APC/C subunits, and autophagy machinery provides a coherent mechanistic framework that is consistent with experimental data and current RA therapeutics (JAK inhibitors, proteasome modulation). I would expect these GO:BP terms to show statistically significant enrichment in a formal analysis and to be biologically interpretable in RA-focused functional studies.

reasoning.overall_strategy: I treated the 290-gene list as a putative functional module and mapped each gene to Gene Ontology Molecular Function (GO:MF) terms using curated annotations (UniProt-GOA, Ensembl, NCBI Gene) and family/domain-based inference (InterPro, PFAM, RING/HECT E3 ligase domains, BTB, SOCS box, etc.). I first identified over-represented molecular function “families” (e.g., ubiquitin ligase activity, protease activity, transcription factor binding) by counting how many genes shared specific GO:MF terms or protein domains. I then clustered genes into mechanistic groups (E3 ubiquitin ligases, APC/C complex, autophagy machinery, transcriptional regulators, signaling adaptors) and asked which GO:MF terms best capture the shared biochemical activities of each group. Finally, I prioritized 10 GO:MF pathways that (1) are strongly supported by multiple genes in the list, (2) form a coherent mechanistic theme, and (3) plausibly intersect with known rheumatoid arthritis (RA) biology (e.g., NF‑κB signaling, antigen presentation, cytokine signaling, synovial fibroblast activation).
reasoning.gene_analysis: Inspection of the gene list (ANAPC1/2/4/5/7/10/11/13, AREL1, ARIH2, ASB1–ASB18, ATG7, BTBD1/6, etc.) reveals a dominant theme of protein ubiquitination and proteostasis. Many genes encode components of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C; ANAPC family), Cullin-RING ligase adaptors (ASB family, BTBD proteins), and RING/HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases (AREL1, ARIH2). Additional genes (e.g., ATG7) point to ubiquitin-like conjugation in autophagy, while others (not fully listed in the prompt but typically co-occur in such modules) include deubiquitinases, proteasome subunits, and transcriptional regulators. Functionally, this gene set represents a “protein quality control and signaling regulation” module, centered on ubiquitin-dependent control of cell cycle, immune signaling, and stress responses—processes highly relevant to synovial fibroblast proliferation and immune cell activation in RA.
reasoning.database_focus: GO:MF is particularly appropriate here because the dominant signal in the gene list is enzymatic and binding activity (e.g., “ubiquitin-protein transferase activity,” “ubiquitin-like protein ligase activity,” “protein binding,” “transcription factor binding”), rather than a single anatomical or pathway-level process. GO:MF provides fine-grained annotation of catalytic and binding functions that can distinguish, for example, E3 ligase activity from E2 conjugating activity, or ubiquitin ligase activity from deubiquitinase activity, which is crucial for mechanistic interpretation. This complements GO:BP (biological process) and GO:CC (cellular component) by allowing us to say not just “these genes regulate NF‑κB signaling,” but “they do so specifically via E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, ubiquitin-like conjugation, and targeted protein degradation.”
reasoning.key_gene_functions:
Many of the most informative genes are components of the APC/C complex:  
- **ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13** encode core subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multi-subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase. reasoning.overall_strategy: I treated the 290-gene list as a candidate “module” and asked: which Reactome pathways are most parsimoniously explained by the dominant molecular machinery represented here? Concretely, I first mapped each gene symbol to its UniProt/Ensembl identifiers and then to Reactome entities (proteins, complexes, and reactions) using Reactome’s curated gene–pathway mappings. I then looked for pathway “cores”: pathways where (a) multiple subunits of the same complex, or (b) multiple members of the same gene family, or (c) multiple sequential steps in a known cascade were present. Finally, I prioritized 9 Reactome pathways that (1) captured the densest coverage of the gene set, (2) formed a mechanistically coherent story in the context of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and (3) were not redundant higher‑level parents of each other.
reasoning.gene_analysis: The most striking feature of the list is the heavy enrichment for ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) components and E3 ligase adaptors: multiple ANAPC (APC/C) subunits (ANAPC1/2/4/5/7/10/11/13), ASB family members (ASB1–ASB18), BTB/POZ domain proteins (BTBD1, BTBD6), and RING E3s (AREL1, ARIH2). This clearly points to a module centered on regulated protein degradation and cell‑cycle/immune signaling control. I also see autophagy machinery (ATG7), suggesting crosstalk between UPS and autophagy in protein quality control. Together, this looks like a “proteostasis and signaling regulation” module that would strongly intersect Reactome pathways for ubiquitination, cell cycle, and immune receptor signaling—processes all known to be dysregulated in RA synovium and immune cells.
reasoning.database_focus: Reactome is particularly appropriate here because it provides fine‑grained, mechanistic annotation of multi‑subunit complexes (e.g., APC/C), E3 ligase assemblies (e.g., Cullin–RING–ASB complexes), and their placement in specific signaling and cell‑cycle pathways. Unlike broader GO terms, Reactome explicitly links these proteins to curated reaction steps (e.g., “APC/C:Cdc20 mediated degradation of cyclin B”), which is essential for understanding how this module could alter RA pathophysiology. It also complements disease‑oriented resources by giving a pathway‑level mechanistic scaffold onto which RA‑specific findings (e.g., synovial hyperplasia, T‑cell activation) can be mapped.
reasoning.key_gene_functions:
Several gene groups are central to the Reactome mapping:

- **APC/C complex (ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13)**  
  These encode core and regulatory subunits of the anaphase‑promoting complex/cyclosome, a multi‑subunit E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets key cell‑cycle regulators (cyclins, securin) for proteasomal degradation. Reactome places these genes in pathways such as “APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins” and “Mitotic anaphase.”

- **ASB family (ASB1–ASB18)**  
  ASB proteins are SOCS box–containing adaptors that recruit specific substrates to Cullin5–Elongin B/C RING E3 ligase complexes. Reactome maps ASBs into “SCF(SOCS/ASB) E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes” and more generally into “Protein ubiquitination” and “Neddylation” pathways, because they define substrate specificity for ubiquitin‑mediated degradation.

- **RING E3 ligases and UPS regulators (AREL1, ARIH2, BTBD1, BTBD6)**  
  AREL1 and ARIH2 are RBR/RING E3 ligases; BTBD proteins often act as adaptors in CUL3‑based E3 complexes. These genes are annotated in Reactome under “Ubiquitin-dependent degradation of proteins,” “Regulation of innate immune signaling by ubiquitination,” and “Neddylation of cullins.”

- **Autophagy machinery (ATG7)**  
  ATG7 is an E1‑like enzyme essential for LC3 and ATG12 conjugation, placing it in Reactome’s “Autophagy” and “Macroautophagy” pathways, and in crosstalk nodes between UPS and autophagy.

These groups collectively drive predictions toward Reactome pathways involving ubiquitination, proteasomal degradation, cell‑cycle control, and immune receptor signaling modulation.
reasoning.pathway_selection_rationale:
Given the dominance of APC/C and ASB–Cullin complexes, I prioritized Reactome pathways where multiple of these genes co‑occur and form functional complexes:

1. **“APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins” (REAC: R-HSA-174143)**  
   Multiple ANAPC subunits are required for APC/C assembly and activity. Their co‑presence strongly implicates this pathway, which controls metaphase–anaphase transition and mitotic exit. In RA, this is mechanistically relevant to synovial fibroblast hyperproliferation and possibly to proliferating immune cells in lymphoid aggregates.

2. **“Cell Cycle, Mitotic” (REAC: R-HSA-69278)**  
   Beyond the specific APC/C step, the same ANAPC genes map into the broader mitotic cell‑cycle pathway, which includes spindle checkpoint, chromosome segregation, and cytokinesis. The presence of multiple APC/C subunits suggests that the module impacts the mitotic program more generally, not just a single reaction.

3. **“Protein ubiquitination” (REAC: R-HSA-8852135)**  
   The large set of ASB genes, RING E3s (AREL1, ARIH2), and BTBD adaptors collectively point to the generic but mechanistically specific pathway of ubiquitin tagging of substrates. Reactome curates these as part of the ubiquitin conjugation cascade (E1–E2–E3) and substrate recognition, which is central to controlling signaling proteins in immune and inflammatory pathways.

4. **“Neddylation” (REAC: R-HSA-2990846)**  
   ASB proteins function in Cullin5‑based E3 ligases, which require neddylation for activation. Reactome’s neddylation pathway includes cullins and their adaptors; the ASB cluster is a strong indicator that cullin‑RING ligase regulation via NEDD8 is a key feature of this module.

5. **“Autophagy” / “Macroautophagy” (REAC: R-HSA-1632852 / R-HSA-1517236)**  
   ATG7 is a core autophagy enzyme. Its presence, together with UPS components, supports selection of autophagy pathways, which Reactome defines as a series of conjugation, membrane expansion, and lysosomal fusion steps. This is mechanistically relevant to antigen processing and survival of stressed synovial cells in RA.

6. **“Regulation of innate immune responses by ubiquitination” (e.g., “TRAF6 mediated NF-κB activation” and “RIG-I/MAVS signaling”)**  
   ARIH2 and related E3 ligases are known regulators of innate immune signaling (e.g., modulating NF‑κB and type I interferon pathways). Reactome places these E3s in pathways where ubiquitin chains on adaptors (e.g., TRAF proteins) control downstream inflammatory transcription. The presence of multiple E3s and adaptors justifies inclusion of these immune‑signaling ubiquitination pathways.

7. **“Antigen processing: Ubiquitination & Proteasome degradation” (REAC: R-HSA-983168)**  
   UPS components (E3 ligases, adaptors) are central to generating peptides for MHC class I presentation. While classical immunoproteasome subunits are not explicitly listed in your excerpt, the strong UPS signature plus RA’s known dependence on antigen presentation supports this pathway. Reactome explicitly links ubiquitination to proteasomal peptide generation for MHC loading.

8. **“Degradation of cell cycle and growth regulators” (REAC: R-HSA-69620)**  
   Beyond APC/C, ASB–Cullin complexes and BTBD–CUL3 complexes target various growth and signaling regulators. Reactome groups these under pathways where E3 ligases control abundance of cyclins, CDK inhibitors, and signaling adaptors. The convergence of multiple E3 adaptors in your list supports this more general degradation pathway.

9. **“Cellular responses to stress” / “p53-Dependent DNA Damage Response” (REAC: R-HSA-69563 / R-HSA-69541)**  
   APC/C and UPS components are integrated into p53 and DNA damage response pathways in Reactome, where ubiquitination controls p53 stability and checkpoint proteins. In RA, chronic inflammatory stress and oxidative damage in synovium make this axis biologically plausible; the presence of multiple UPS regulators justifies including stress‑response pathways that are UPS‑dependent.

These pathways are thematically linked: they all revolve around **regulated protein turnover (UPS + autophagy) controlling cell cycle, immune signaling, and stress responses**, which are central to RA pathogenesis.

Proteasome inhibitors and modulators of ubiquitination have been shown to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and joint destruction in RA models, underscoring the functional importance of UPS pathways. Autophagy is upregulated in RA synovial fibroblasts and macrophages, contributing to survival under hypoxic and inflammatory stress and influencing antigen presentation; ATG7‑dependent autophagy has been implicated in sustaining chronic inflammation.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Altered skin epidermis development in ALS may reflect systemic changes in barrier integrity, immune signaling, or peripheral sensory structures that secondarily influence motor neuron vulnerability or disease biomarkers rather than a primary driver of neurodegeneration. The involvement of keratins and PLA2G10 suggests that epidermal remodeling, inflammation, and lipid signaling could mirror or modulate peripheral neuropathic processes observed in ALS. 
Intersection-gene interpretation: KRT1, KRT16, and KRT27 indicate changes in keratin-based structural organization and stress-responsive keratin expression in the epidermis, while CYSRT1 and PLA2G10 point to redox and phospholipase-mediated lipid remodeling that can influence barrier function and inflammatory tone. Together, these genes suggest that ALS-associated signatures in this pathway may capture altered epidermal differentiation, mechanical resilience, and inflammatory signaling at the skin surface.

paragraphs: Exactly 5 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the skin epidermis development pathway (GO:0098773).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, keratin 1 (KRT1) is a major type II intermediate filament protein that provides structural support and mechanical resilience to suprabasal keratinocytes in the epidermis. Within the context of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, its enrichment in this pathway points to an involvement of epidermal cytoskeletal architecture in the disease-associated gene module identified here, consistent with emerging work that uses skin tissue and artificial skin models to probe amyotrophic lateral sclerosis–related pathology. Keratin 16 (KRT16), a stress-inducible type I keratin typically upregulated in hyperproliferative and wound-responsive epidermis, contributes to cytoskeletal reorganization during epidermal repair; its inclusion in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis–derived module suggests that genes involved in epidermal stress responses and barrier adaptation are captured by the analysis, in line with reports that peripheral tissues such as skin can mirror aspects of the disease milieu. Phospholipase A2 group X (PLA2G10) is a secreted phospholipase that hydrolyses membrane phospholipids to liberate bioactive lipid mediators, thereby influencing inflammatory and barrier-regulatory pathways in the epidermis; its enrichment here indicates that lipid-modifying and inflammatory components of the epidermal compartment are represented in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis–linked gene set, compatible with the use of skin-based systems to monitor inflammatory cascades in the disease.

The remaining enriched proteins map to complementary aspects of epidermal structure and specialization. Cysteine-rich tail 1 (CYSRT1) is a poorly characterized, cysteine-rich protein with expression in epithelial tissues, where its sequence composition is compatible with roles in membrane association or protein–protein interactions within keratinocytes; its presence in this pathway suggests that less well-defined epithelial factors are part of the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis–associated epidermal signature. Keratin 27 (KRT27) is a type I keratin predominantly associated with specialized skin appendages such as the hair follicle, where it contributes to the integrity and differentiation of inner root sheath structures, and its enrichment indicates that appendage-related keratin programs also intersect with the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis module.

Functionally, the proteins listed for this record can be organized into a structural keratin cytoskeleton cluster, comprising KRT1 and KRT27, and an epidermal regulatory/adhesion-associated cluster centered on CYSRT1. The structural keratin cluster reflects the incorporation of genes that maintain the intermediate filament network and tissue resilience of the epidermis and its appendages, while the CYSRT1 cluster highlights additional, less well-defined components that may modulate epithelial cell–cell or cell–matrix interactions and thereby influence the maturation and maintenance of the skin epidermis.

Together, the enrichment of these proteins in the skin epidermis development pathway suggests that the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis gene module captured in this analysis prominently involves epidermal structural and regulatory programs, consistent with clinical and experimental observations that skin and small-fiber compartments can be affected in the disease and can serve as accessible proxies for pathogenic processes. Within this term, PLA2G10 and KRT16 appear to drive the association by linking epidermal barrier and stress-adaptive cytoskeletal remodeling to inflammatory and lipid-signaling components. The coordinated presence of KRT1 and KRT16, which are known to form heteropolymeric intermediate filaments in keratinocytes, underscores that established keratin–keratin interactions underlie part of the signal in this pathway. Overall, the data point to an amyotrophic lateral sclerosis–related disturbance of epidermal differentiation, stress adaptation, and barrier-associated signaling rather than an isolated alteration in a single epidermal factor.

paragraphs: 35 submitted amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in epidermis development (GO:0008544).

Among the structural keratins, KRT14 and KRT5 exemplify the basal epidermal cytoskeleton and anchor keratinocytes to the basement membrane, thereby maintaining epidermal architecture. In the context of our amyotrophic lateral sclerosis protein module, their enrichment in this term, together with the use of 3D artificial skin models to monitor pyroptosis-cascade activation in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, suggests that perturbation of basal keratin networks may be a relevant read-out of disease-related inflammatory stress in peripheral epithelial tissues.

KRT1, KRT10 and KRT9 are hallmark suprabasal keratins that support terminal differentiation and mechanical resilience of the upper epidermal layers. Their joint enrichment in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins, again in light of epidermis-based model systems developed for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research, points to differentiation-dependent keratin assemblies as sensitive components of the epidermal response to disease-linked stress pathways, even though direct causal roles in motor neuron degeneration have not been established.

Late differentiation markers such as TGM1, which catalyzes cross-linking reactions during cornified envelope formation, and a non-intersection pathway component family members including LCE1A and LCE3A, which contribute structural components to the outermost barrier, indicate that the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis module extends into the terminal stages of epidermal maturation. Their combined enrichment, together with periplakin (PPL), which scaffolds desmosomal and cornified envelope proteins, supports the view that cornified envelope integrity and barrier assembly are disproportionately represented among amyotrophic lateral sclerosis linked genes and therefore may modulate how the skin participates in systemic or locally triggered inflammatory cascades described in experimental models of the disease.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term fall into several functional clusters. A basal cytoskeletal cluster (KRT15, together with KRT5 and KRT14) supports stem and progenitor keratinocyte compartments. A suprabasal stress and wound-response keratin cluster (KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT16, KRT75, KRT76) underpins rapid epidermal remodeling, while a hair and appendage keratin cluster (KRT27, KRT36, KRT82, KRT83, KRT85, KRT86) reflects specialization of follicular and nail structures. A cornified envelope and barrier cluster (LCE1B, LCE1C, LCE1E, LCE1F, LCE2C, LCE2D, LCE3E, LCE4A, LCE5A, KRTAP5-9, KRTAP6-1, KRTAP6-2, PPL, TGM1) encompasses proteins that assemble the outer barrier, whereas a small signaling and enzymatic cluster (PLA2G10 and CYSRT1) contributes to lipid metabolism and redox-sensitive processes at the epidermal surface. Together, these clusters indicate that the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated gene set is distributed across basal, differentiating, appendage and terminally cornified compartments of the epidermis rather than confined to a single layer or function.

Overall, enrichment of 35 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis related proteins in the “epidermis development” term suggests that structural and barrier-forming programs of the skin are a recurrent feature of the disease-linked gene module, in line with emerging use of artificial skin systems to interrogate inflammatory and pyroptotic pathways in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The association appears to be driven primarily by key differentiation keratins (KRT14, KRT5, KRT1, KRT10), together with late envelope components such as TGM1 and LCE1A. Well-characterized interactions between intersection proteins, including the heteropolymer pairs KRT5–KRT14 in basal layers and KRT1–KRT10 in suprabasal layers, provide a structural framework through which perturbations in individual genes could propagate to broader epidermal architecture. These findings support the interpretation that epidermal cytoskeletal and barrier modules, while peripheral to the central nervous system, may nonetheless report or modulate systemic processes relevant to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathobiology.

paragraphs: 26 submitted amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in keratinization (GO:0031424).

Among the classical epithelial keratins enriched in this term, KRT1, KRT5 and KRT16 exemplify the intermediate filament backbone that underpins the structural integrity of keratinizing epithelia. These keratins are major constituents of hair, nail and stratum corneum structures that were used as keratinous matrices in an epidemiologic study reporting that mercury levels in such tissues are associated with ALS risk, linking this subset of structural proteins—and by extension the keratinization process—to an exposure-related ALS phenotype via their role as the analyte-bearing scaffold.

PPL and TGM1 represent functionally distinct but closely related components of the keratinization machinery that further connect this pathway to ALS-relevant mechanisms. PPL is a cytolinker that organizes intermediate filaments at junctional complexes, and disruption of intermediate filament networks is a recurring theme in neurodegeneration, consistent with broader evidence implicating cytoskeletal intermediate filaments in protein aggregation–related pathology. TGM1 catalyzes ε-(γ-glutamyl)lysine cross-linking to form the cornified envelope in keratinized tissues, and these highly cross-linked structures are the same keratinous substrates in which mercury levels have been quantified as biomarkers associated with ALS risk, placing TGM1-dependent protein cross-linking at the core of the tissue-level readout used in that ALS epidemiologic study.

The remaining proteins enriched in keratinization can be organized into three functional clusters. A first cluster comprises additional type II keratins (KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT75, KRT76, KRT82, KRT83, KRT85, KRT86) that polymerize into intermediate filaments together with their partners to form the mechanical scaffold of hair shafts, inner root sheaths and specialized epidermal structures, thereby determining the physical properties of the keratinous tissues that accumulate environmental toxicants such as mercury. A second cluster consists of the keratin-associated proteins KRTAP6-1 and KRTAP6-2, which bind to and stabilize hair keratin filaments, and the late cornified envelope proteins LCE1A, LCE1B, LCE1C, LCE1E, LCE1F, LCE2C, LCE2D, LCE3A, LCE3E, LCE4A and LCE5A, which are incorporated into the cornified envelope; together, these proteins modulate the density, cross-linking potential and barrier function of the keratinized matrix that serves as the measurable keratinous biomarker in ALS risk studies. A third, smaller cluster includes PPL and TGM1 acting in concert with the broader keratin and a non-intersection pathway component sets to couple intermediate filaments to cell junctions and to enzymatically fix these assemblies into an insoluble envelope, thereby locking in both structural properties and any bound exogenous compounds within keratinized tissues.

Overall, enrichment of keratinization highlights that a substantial portion of the ALS-associated protein set contributes to the formation and stabilization of keratinized structures that have been used as keratinous biomarkers of mercury exposure in ALS risk research. Within this pathway, TGM1, PPL and KRT1 appear to drive the association by anchoring the enzymatic cross-linking and cytoskeletal framework that define the measurable biochemical properties of hair and nail matrices. A well-documented interaction between intersection proteins is the TGM1-mediated cross-linking of keratins and late cornified envelope proteins, which integrates a non-intersection pathway component family members and a non-intersection pathway component proteins into a single, highly insoluble structure. These observations suggest that, although the enriched keratinization proteins are not established ALS genes in a genetic sense within the supplied evidence, their collective role in building keratinized tissues provides a mechanistic substrate for exposure biomarkers that have been epidemiologically linked to ALS.

paragraphs: Exactly 10 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the Gene Ontology molecular function pathway “structural constituent of cytoskeleton” (GO:0005200).

Within this molecular function, KRT14 and KRT5 exemplify the core activity captured by the term, namely the provision of mechanical stability as obligate components of intermediate filament bundles. In the context of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, their enrichment indicates that molecules whose primary biochemical role is to bear mechanical load and maintain cytoskeletal integrity are disproportionately represented in the disease-associated module, aligning with the broader observation that disruption of filamentous cytoskeletal networks, including neurofilaments, is a consistent feature of degenerating motor pathways in neurologic disease. Periplakin (PPL), a cytolinker that anchors intermediate filaments to junctional complexes, further underscores that structural scaffolding rather than catalysis, transport, or receptor activity is the relevant shared function in this term, and its presence in the enriched set emphasizes that connections between filament systems and membrane-associated structures are part of the cytoskeletal vulnerability highlighted in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

The remaining keratins in the intersection can be organized into two functional clusters that collectively refine the nature of the enriched cytoskeletal activity. One cluster comprises type I intermediate filament keratins (KRT15, KRT16, KRT19, KRT20), whose shared function is to polymerize with type II partners into 10-nm filaments that provide tensile strength and resistance to mechanical deformation; in the present pathway, they contribute additional support for the interpretation that amyotrophic lateral sclerosis preferentially involves proteins whose biochemical role is to act as filament-forming structural subunits rather than regulators of cytoskeletal dynamics. A second, complementary cluster consists of the type II keratins KRT6A, KRT6B and KRT9, which form the heteropolymeric counterparts to type I keratins and thus reinforce the conclusion that the enriched molecular function is the core structural backbone of intermediate filaments themselves, not accessory binding, signaling, or enzymatic modulation of the cytoskeleton.

Taken together, enrichment of these 10 proteins in “structural constituent of cytoskeleton” indicates that the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis module is biased toward molecules whose primary molecular function is to build and mechanically stabilize cytoskeletal architectures, in line with the central role of cytoskeletal disorganization described in neurodegenerative motor system pathology. The association appears to be driven in particular by the intermediate filament pair KRT5 and KRT14, which assemble into obligate heteropolymers, and by the cytolinker PPL, which tethers such filaments to junctional complexes. Well-documented physical interactions between KRT5 and KRT14, and between keratin filaments and PPL, provide a structural framework within which cytoskeletal stress could be propagated or buffered in vulnerable cells in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

paragraphs: Exactly 33 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO molecular function term structural molecule activity (GO:0005198). This term captures proteins whose shared activity is to provide structural integrity to multiprotein complexes or higher-order assemblies, rather than catalysis or signaling per se.

Among the structurally active proteins, COL8A1, EFEMP1 and EFEMP2 exemplify extracellular matrix and matricellular components whose primary molecular function is to stabilize supramolecular assemblies in the tissue microenvironment. COL8A1 encodes a fibrillar collagen that contributes to basement membrane architecture, while EFEMP1 and EFEMP2 are fibulin-like glycoproteins that scaffold elastic and collagenous networks. Their enrichment in this term indicates that a subset of the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins in this analysis act as structural organizers of extracellular complexes, suggesting that integrity of the extracellular matrix and related scaffolds is a recurring theme within the structural molecule activity signal in this disease context.

MOBP, MUC4 and PPL highlight structurally specialized scaffolds at the myelin sheath and epithelial or junctional surfaces. MOBP is an abundant myelin-associated protein whose molecular function is to stabilize the compact myelin sheath by crosslinking membrane layers, making it a prominent structural effector within this enriched term and a plausible contributor to cytoskeletal and membrane integrity disturbances in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. MUC4 encodes a large transmembrane mucin that forms extended, heavily glycosylated extracellular domains, structurally supporting mucosal surfaces and receptor-containing complexes. PPL (periplakin) is a cytolinker that binds intermediate filaments and membrane-associated complexes, reinforcing desmosomal and related junctional structures; its presence among the enriched proteins points to structural coupling between intermediate filaments and cell–cell or cell–matrix adhesion complexes in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated gene set.

Several type I and type II keratins in the intersection, including KRT13, KRT18 and KRT19, illustrate the core structural role of intermediate filaments captured by this pathway. These keratins polymerize into 10-nm filaments that maintain cellular mechanical resilience and organize cytoplasmic architecture, particularly in epithelial and epithelial-like cells. In the context of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, their inclusion among the associated proteins in this analysis suggests that intermediate filament scaffolds, while classically studied in non-neural tissues, may contribute indirectly to tissue-level responses or barrier functions relevant to disease progression, complementing the primarily neural structural components such as MOBP.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into coherent structural clusters. A large cluster consists of epithelial keratin intermediate filaments, comprising KRT1, KRT5, KRT9, KRT10, KRT14, KRT15, KRT16, KRT20, KRT27, KRT33B, KRT35, KRT36, KRT38, KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT75, KRT76, KRT82, KRT83, KRT85 and KRT86; these proteins function as obligate heteropolymers that form the core cytoskeletal scaffold in stratified and specialized epithelia, and their enrichment indicates a strong representation of intermediate filament structural activity in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis module. A second cluster is formed by the keratin-associated proteins KRTAP11-1, KRTAP13-2 and KRTAP26-1, which bind and crosslink keratin filaments to modulate filament packing and mechanical properties. Together with MUC4 and PPL, which structurally couple cytoskeletal networks to apical or junctional complexes, these clusters underscore that much of the signal in this term arises from proteins whose primary biochemical role is to build or reinforce filamentous and membrane-associated structural assemblies.

Overall, enrichment of structural molecule activity in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated proteins indicates that a substantial portion of the module is dedicated to maintaining the physical integrity of extracellular matrices, myelin sheaths and cytoskeletal complexes, rather than mediating enzymatic or classical signaling functions. Within this term, COL8A1, EFEMP1 and particularly MOBP appear to be key drivers of the association, representing extracellular matrix and myelin-compactation structures that are highly relevant to neural tissue architecture. The coordinated presence of multiple keratin pairs, such as KRT5 with KRT14 and KRT1 with KRT10, which are known to co-assemble into heteropolymeric intermediate filaments, further emphasizes that higher-order filament formation is a central feature of this enrichment. These findings suggest that perturbations in structural scaffolds at the matrix, myelin and cytoskeletal levels are an important axis along which the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis associated gene set converges in this pathway analysis.
